articles.title: Measuring Merit in College Admissions
articles.abstract: I discuss the concepts of merit and meritocracy as they apply to college admissions in the U.S., paying particular attention to the question of whether standardized tests should be regarded as measures of merit. Several factors—the Varsity Blues cheating scandal, the pandemic, and an increasing awareness of systemic racism—have led to a dramatic move away from test requirements: Most U.S. colleges do not currently require admissions tests. Traditionalists have deplored this change, viewing test scores as a central pillar of meritocratic admissions. However, critics of the traditional view have advocated for emphasizing such qualities as creativity, ethical behavior, and communication skills in selecting applicants, arguing that these characteristics are, in fact, aspects of merit. Finally, some scholars have maintained that meritocratic selection need not involve either academic criteria or aspects of character. From this perspective, the definition of merit is entirely dependent on the goals of the institution.

articles.title: Power and Organizational Opacity in College Admissions
articles.abstract: Top American colleges balance ideals of meritocracy and racial diversity to make admissions decisions. But recent legal and political challenges undermine their ability to openly pursue racial diversity. What will be the likely effect of these challenges? In this speculative article, we argue that the long-term impact on student body composition is likely to be limited at schools that continue to prioritize racial diversity, as a result of organizational opacity : the capacity of complex organizations to obscure their activities from outsiders. We speculate that mounting external pressures will lead admissions offices to manipulate an increasingly complex set of organizational levers to pursue both meritocracy and diversity, at least to the extent that both continue to be valued as worthwhile ideals. While often effective, increasing opacity will also carry significant risks for colleges and universities, which we discuss.

articles.title: Meritocracy and Higher Education in the United States
articles.abstract: This article disambiguates different conceptions of merit to consider whether higher education is currently, or could plausibly become, meritocratic. We argue that contemporary societies are not meritocratic in the commonly popularized sense and that because society is not meritocratic, college admissions could not be. Calls for college admissions to be meritocratic demand that they reward developed abilities, not native abilities, which makes meritocracy impossible in societies that maintain the institution of the family. Next, we explain why meritocracy, so understood, would be undesirable even if it were possible. Further, we argue that even societies that are not meritocratic may instantiate some of the damaging features associated with meritocracy, because those features are a consequence of people believing their society is meritocratic—thus, the irony that basing elite college admissions on “merit” may cause further harms because it exacerbates the (false) belief that society is meritocratic.

articles.title: Stratification by Design: Meritocracy and the Reproduction of Inequality
articles.abstract: Meritocracy is often celebrated as a fair system in which social positions are distributed according to individual ability rather than inherited privilege. Yet, evidence shows that meritocratic systems routinely reproduce inequality. I argue that such outcomes are not failures of meritocracy but constitutive features of how it operates. Drawing on existing research, I identify three mechanisms through which elites sustain their dominance in ostensibly merit-based systems: consecration (power to define and evaluate merit), adaptation (unequal capacity to cultivate valued traits), and co-optation (strategic use of meritocratic ideals to resist challenges to privilege). I further contend that the underlying premise of meritocracy—that some individuals are more deserving than others—legitimizes social hierarchies and can result in the dehumanization of marginalized groups. I conclude by arguing that genuine fairness requires not only less biased measures of merit but also deeper structural transformations that reduce the high stakes of social stratification.

articles.title: Inhabited Professions: How Cultural Norms of Excellence Anchor Inequality in Professions
articles.abstract: To advance understanding of how cultural notions of merit in professions perpetuate inequality, we introduce the novel concept of “inhabited professions.” We argue that notions of professional merit play out within day-to-day interactions among workplace colleagues in ways that generate negative consequences for those who deviate from predominant conceptions of excellence. As a case, we focus on how a particular professional norm, the (de)valuation of diversity concerns, shapes gender inequality in STEM departments. Using data from 266 academic scientists nested in 14 departments, we find that women with a substantial gap between their personal concern for diversity and their colleagues’ beliefs about the importance of promoting diversity are significantly more likely to report chilly departmental climates, to feel disrespected, and to intend to leave the university than men in their departments. While women defenders of diversity are treated as less worthy, men diversity proponents are buffered from these negative consequences.

articles.title: Meritocratic Pay Beliefs in the Contemporary United States
articles.abstract: What do workers think should determine their pay? And what do they think does determine their pay? We analyze prior surveys of U.S. workers and an original 2025 survey to assess pay beliefs, finding widespread and long-standing support for meritocratic pay principles. Since the early 1990s, majorities of full-time workers subscribe to the idea that pay should be based at least in part on job performance, and in 2025 nearly half of workers report that individual performance should be the main factor determining their pay. Results are generally consistent across key sociodemographic and labor market characteristics, although women are significantly more likely to believe their performance should be the most important determinant of their pay, and public sector workers and union members are less likely to believe that their pay is performance-based. We conclude by assessing the policy implications of these meritocratic pay norms.

articles.title: Caste and Meritocracy in India
articles.authors: Bishnupriya Gupta, Kaivan Munshi, Swapnil Singh
articles.abstract: The caste system in India acts as a barrier to meritocracy. For centuries the lowest castes were disadvantaged socially and economically. Evidence from the colonial censuses of the early twentieth century shows large differences in literacy and occupation between the highest and the lowest castes. After independence, India adopted affirmative action in state-funded education and public sector jobs that benefited people in the so-called scheduled castes and tribes, who were the disadvantaged groups. We show that since the 1980s, there has been convergence in education and occupation between the upper castes and that population.

articles.title: From State-Sponsored to Market-Driven Meritocracy? Changes in the French Education System and Higher Education Admissions
articles.abstract: This article presents an analysis of changes to the concept of meritocracy in France, highlighting the interrelation of social configurations and how they influence the definition and enactment of merit. I present a macro-level analysis of changing conceptions of merit and a micro-level one of how these changes have been implemented in the admissions process of a prestigious higher education institution. I argue that in the past two decades, there has been a partial but significant replacement of a state-sponsored meritocracy by a market-driven one. This change has led to a hybridization of the aristocratic, scholastic, and market-oriented cultural criteria that are used to appraise students’ merit and also to the development of private services and devices alongside public ones. These processes have not altered the unequal pattern of vertical stratification in France but instead have introduced new “horizontal” movements in the social space.

articles.title: The Siamese Crocodiles: Meritocratic Equilibria in African Perspective
articles.abstract: The notion of meritocracy is in crisis in the Western world, with scholars and citizens arguing that it creates a divisive equilibrium with high levels of inequality and cultural polarization. We argue that the meritocratic equilibrium that is currently being scrutinized is more culturally embedded than its critics recognize. We show that in Africa, for example, beliefs, practices, and norms allow for the existence of an equilibrium that is genuinely meritocratic and also redistributive. We show how African cultures tend to combine individualism and communalism, and that in achieving this balance, Africans innovated different norms and mechanisms that attempt to harmonize the interests of the individual with those of the community. These mechanisms do appear to break down in parts of Africa where witchcraft is used as a mechanism for enforcing the social contract.

articles.title: Meritocracy and the Networks It Forged: China’s Imperial Examination
articles.abstract: Institutions that claim to reward merit often also serve as engines that drive the formation of important social networks. We examine this dual role in China’s imperial examination, one of history’s longest-lived systems of meritocracy. We draw on the exam performance data of 24,269 individuals across 112 national examinations in the Qing dynasty (1644–1905) to trace who among them rose to become top officials in the dynasty. Strong exam performance increased the likelihood of attaining high office, but advancement also depended on individuals’ ties to powerful examiners. Because performance and ties to powerful examiners were strongly complementary, individuals’ success appeared to rest on merit even as social networks played a role. And after the dramatic political changes of the 1840s, ties to powerful examiners still remained influential, although the influential examiners themselves changed. These findings help to explain why such systems retain legitimacy even when networks matter greatly.

articles.title: Latin America’s Persistent Disorder: Meritocracy Without Mobility
articles.abstract: Latin America combines strong beliefs in meritocracy with persistently high inequality, crime, and informality. Explaining this “meritocracy without mobility” requires understanding how institutions, culture, and social norms jointly sustain an unfair and inefficient equilibrium. We argue that this equilibrium rests on three mutually reinforcing foundations: deep mistrust of public institutions, low interpersonal trust, and an untamed individualism that privileges private over collective solutions. These cultural and normative forces weaken provision of public goods, normalize rule-breaking, and preserve belief in meritocracy despite low social mobility. Meritocracy is largely imagined but nonetheless fits this individualistic culture, legitimizing the status quo. It is also perversely validated by limited mobility in the widely accepted informal, and at times illegal, economy. These dynamics help explain why reforms often fail to provide widely beneficial outcomes, as they cannot surmount weak institutions and entrenched beliefs, social norms, and practices. articles.authors: Steven N. Durlauf, James A. Robinson

articles.title: The State and Gender Equality: Sweden—Model or Aberration?
articles.abstract: The Nordic countries are leaders in gender equality in the workplace and in the home. Why is this the case? State capacity, this article argues. For the most part, modern states seek to reduce the extent to which ascriptive traits establish status in the population, because ascriptive power hierarchies distort meritocratic talent allocation and thus economic progress. This article places gender equality in a long line of state-led policies that level the salience of ascriptive traits, on par with the abolition of noble and servile statuses, equality before the law, and the expansion of suffrage. I review the economic and political arguments for equality—including gender equality—in comparative historical context, focusing on Sweden as a case in point of how Nordic countries’ high state legitimacy and bureaucratic capacity have allowed them to chip away at gender roles, which are arguably the last bastion of ascriptive status.

articles.title: Strategic Inversion: How Refugees Reconfigure Everyday Resistance under Benevolent Oppression
articles.authors: Rekha Krishnan, Aloysius Marcus Kahindi, Rajiv Krishnan Kozhikode
articles.abstract: What does everyday resistance look like among dominated populations experiencing paternalistic care rather than extraction? Research on everyday resistance emerged from contexts where power extracts surplus from the oppressed. In this scholarship, the backstage is a space where the dominated cultivate hidden transcripts to cope with oppression, while the frontstage, where performances are enacted to those in power, is primary. Inversions of this order, when they occur, are momentary. Using ethnographic fieldwork in two Tanzanian refugee camps, we show that under benevolent oppression—control justified by paternalistic care rather than extraction—dominated populations respond through “strategic inversion”: a reordering of dramaturgical space where the backstage is primary and the frontstage remains tactical. Refugees moved the center of social life backstage, into a thriving underground economy, and kept up frontstage displays of helplessness to shield it. Within this alternative social order, competition and cooperation operated as two routes to heshima (dignity/deference). Competition resisted the uniformity of the refugee label, and cooperation rejected the helplessness it presumed. Refugees sustained this inversion through compliance flooding , rule-following performances so dense that officials could not tell forbidden from permitted activity; embedded enforcement , as guards became accomplices in maintaining the clandestine economy they policed; and collective coordination , where communities maintained alert systems and consistent performances to shield backstage activities. Our analysis extends research on everyday resistance by demonstrating that under benevolent oppression, subordinates actively build and experience empowerment, rather than merely imagining alternative moral orders or experiencing them briefly in bounded rituals.

articles.title: Organizational Consolidation: How Organizations Reflect or Refract Societal Hierarchies
articles.abstract: To understand how organizations distribute resources, we need to understand how they come to evaluate their members as worthy. This article introduces “organizational consolidation”: the degree to which ascriptive statuses—race, gender, class—align with the context-specific criteria that actors use when evaluating one another. Building on relational inequality theory and inhabited institutionalism, we argue that organizational consolidation shapes which attributes stand out, how actors categorize one another, and how combinations of attributes yield recognition or marginalization. When consolidation is high, local meaning-making is more likely to reproduce patterns of recognition that track ascriptive statuses; when it is low, alternative patterns become possible. We develop a concept-methods package that turns this framework into a roadmap for observing local patterns of recognition: association rule mining, latent class analysis, and partial order set modeling. We illustrate the value of these tools in a small, racially diverse U.S. high school where consolidation is low: teachers evaluate students through combinations of race, gender, and organizationally relevant characteristics, rather than any single attribute. By formalizing organizational consolidation as a measurable structural condition, we provide a diagnostic for comparing how organizations reflect or refract broader social hierarchies—shifting focus to how and under what organizational conditions inequality takes the specific forms it does.

articles.title: Policy as a Bargaining Outcome: Coalition Leverage and Pledge Fulfillment
articles.authors: Mark A. Kayser, Jochen Rehmert, Petra Schleiter
articles.abstract: Which parties can deliver the policies that they promised? In multiparty contexts, parties must bargain to realize electoral promises. Prior work shows that parties influence policy change by using resources such as legislative seats, ministerial posts, and agenda, veto, and policing powers, while only theoretical work considers parties’ bargaining leverage from potentially changing the government. But for parties, fulfilling pledges (not incremental policy change) is paramount and they use their full leverage to achieve it. We offer and test a more complete and politically relevant account of multiparty policymaking that includes parties’ bargaining leverage through coalition options and focuses on the realization of distinct policy promises. We estimate regression analyses of pledge fulfillment in nine parliamentary democracies from 1974 to 2011 as well as local average treatment effects across a discontinuity and find that parties’ bargaining leverage from potential coalition change trumps conventional explanations for policy outcomes.

articles.title: The Audience of Coalition Bargaining: Voter Reactions to Portfolio Allocation
articles.authors: Ida B. Hjermitslev, Mathias Wessel Tromborg
articles.abstract: Obtaining portfolios is one of the most important pay-offs that parties receive from getting into office. Accordingly, we know a lot about how portfolios are distributed between coalition partners, but surprisingly little about how voters react to these distributional outcomes. We address this research gap both theoretically and empirically. Theoretically, we argue that voters use cues from the quantitative and qualitative portfolio distributions to evaluate coalition partners’ competence in negotiations, which in turn shapes party support. Empirically, we use original experimental and panel survey data from the 2022 Danish general election. We find that voters infer negotiation competence from the number, power, and party-specific salience of the portfolios a party obtains. We also demonstrate that many voters paid attention to the real-world negotiation outcome and withdrew their support for the parties they perceived handled the negotiations less competently.

articles.title: Reshaping Belonging: National Identity Change in Post-Referendum Britain
articles.authors: Jac M. Larner, James David Griffiths, Daniel Wincott
articles.abstract: National identity is usually treated as a stable driver of political behaviour, yet we know little about whether it responds to major political events. We examine how two pivotal electoral events – the 2014 Scottish Independence Referendum and the 2016 EU Referendum – were associated with changes in citizens’ sense of national belonging. Using the 2014–2025 British Election Study Internet Panel, we show that both referendums precipitated significant shifts in national identification, primarily among those on the losing side. Post-referendum changes in Scotland proved temporary, but among Remain voters British identification fell substantially and remained depressed through 2025, with the gap between winners and losers widening over time. These findings suggest national identity is more event-sensitive than commonly assumed, and that divisive referendums may leave durable marks on how citizens in multinational states relate to the state by eroding shared national sentiment.

articles.title: Inhibitory Institutions: The Tradeoffs of Public Goods Quantity and Quality
articles.abstract: Governments frequently invest in public goods that citizens don’t want, yet voters hesitate to punish politicians who build useless or corrupt projects. I introduce the concept of inhibitory institutions—rules that allow state or societal actors to review, obstruct, or veto public investments before they are approved—and argue that they improve public goods quality at the cost of reduced quantity. This quantity-quality tradeoff binds most tightly when bureaucrats enjoy career autonomy from politicians and political competition encourages institutional enforcement. I illustrate the tradeoff through case studies of metro projects in Bogotá and Lima, where divergent institutional conditions led to contrasting outcomes for the quantity and quality of construction. Quantitative evidence from local infrastructure projects in Colombia suggests that political alliances to bypass inhibitory rules increase spending but reduce quality. At a time when observers want to cut procedural checks to get things built, this article underscores the risks for what gets built.

articles.title: Promoting Women to Managerial Roles in the Bangladeshi Garment Sector
articles.authors: Rocco Macchiavello, Andreas Menzel, Atonu Rabbani, Christopher Woodruff
articles.abstract: Women remain disadvantaged in promotion to managerial positions. We conduct a field experiment with 24 large garment factories in Bangladesh to test for inefficient representation of women among line supervisors. We identify the marginal female and male candidates for supervisory positions and randomly assign them to manage production lines. We document four findings: (1) In contrast to widespread negative beliefs about women's ability as supervisors at baseline, female candidates selected by the factories had similar skills to males; (2) during the trial, females performed worse than males, which we show is related to negative bias against them; (3) after the trial, however, many female candidates were retained as supervisors and, conditional on that, performed similar to males; and (4) after the end of our intervention, factories permanently increased the share of women among newly appointed supervisors. A conceptual framework of experimentation over discrimination rationalizes all these facts and cautions against the standard logic to test for discrimination: when there is uncertainty about the performance of the discriminated group, equal—or even worse—performance of the marginal candidates of that group is no longer sufficient to rule out inefficient discrimination.

articles.title: The Role of Trade in Premature Deindustrialization and Industry Polarization
articles.authors: Michael Sposi, Kei-Mu Yi, Jing Zhang
articles.abstract: We document two key patterns of structural change: premature deindustrialization and rising industry polarization. Using a dynamic open‐economy model with sector‐biased technological change (SBTC), we evaluate the role of trade in these shifts. Trade alone does not cause premature deindustrialization, but its interaction with SBTC—transmitting global technological change, amplifying the decline in manufacturing's relative price over time, and generating manufacturing trade imbalances across countries—deepens premature deindustrialization over time. Industry polarization, by contrast, emerges only through trade‐driven specialization, as countries diverge along lines of comparative advantage.

articles.title: Physician Behavior in the Presence of a Secondary Market: The Case of Prescription Opioids
articles.abstract: This paper examines how drug diversion influences the prescribing practices of physicians and the equilibrium health impacts of prescription medications. Focusing on the case of prescription opioids, a commonly prescribed and frequently diverted medication at the heart of the worst drug crisis in U.S. history, I design and estimate a model of physician behavior in the presence of a secondary market with patient search. To access prescription opioids for medical purposes or misuse, patients search over physicians on the legal primary market or turn to an illegal secondary market. Physicians, who care both about their impact on population health and their revenue from office visits, take into account the possibility that patients might resell their prescriptions on the secondary market when prescribing. The model demonstrates that the potential for diversion will tend to make strict physicians more hesitant in their prescribing while leading lenient prescribers to loosen their prescription thresholds, thereby exacerbating prescribing differences between more and less lenient physicians. Estimates reveal that the presence of a secondary market induces most physicians to be more careful in their prescribing, which brings prescriptions closer to their optimal level, but also causes harm through the reallocation of prescriptions for abuse.

articles.title: Security Design Under Common‐Value Competition
articles.abstract: This paper studies security design by bidders with dispersed information about a common‐value investment opportunity. Among a broad set of securities, bidders offer debt financing—the flattest securities. A first reason is that debt mitigates bidders' exposure to the winner's curse when there are two bidders. Second, the entrepreneur either has an informational advantage initially or gains one by inferring from the bids, and is more likely to select debt offers when optimistic about the project. While a bidder's choice of security also has a signaling effect, this effect is dominated by the winner's curse and informed‐selection effects, and does not affect the equilibrium outcome. These results contrast sharply with security design by a monopolistic investor, as well as with DeMarzo, Kremer, and Skrzypacz's (2005) results under private‐value competition. The entrepreneur's ability to commit to an ordered set of securities does not improve revenue.

articles.title: Causal Inference for Spatial Treatments
articles.abstract: Many events and policies (treatments) occur at specific spatial locations, with researchers interested in their effects on nearby units. I approach the spatial treatment setting from an experimental perspective: What ideal experiment would we design to estimate the causal effects of spatial treatments? This perspective motivates a comparison between units near realized treatment locations and units near counterfactual (unrealized) candidate locations, which differs from current empirical practice. I derive design‐based standard errors that are straightforward to compute. For observational data, I propose machine learning methods to find counterfactual candidate locations when observable characteristics, rather than potential outcomes, determine treatment probabilities. To accommodate methods for high‐dimensional data in the theory, I extend a double machine learning result to the design‐based framework with spatial correlations. I apply the proposed methods to study the causal effects of grocery stores on foot traffic to nearby businesses during COVID‐19 shelter‐in‐place policies, finding a large positive effect at very short distances, with no effect at larger distances.

articles.title: Screening Property Rights for Innovation
articles.abstract: We develop a dynamic structural model of patent screening incorporating incentives, intrinsic motivation, and multiround negotiation. We use natural language processing to create a measure of patent distance, which together with detailed data on examiner decisions, enables us to estimate the model and study strategic decisions by applicants and examiners. Using the estimated model, we quantify the effectiveness of the U.S. Patent Office and evaluate counterfactual policy reforms. We find that patent screening is moderately effective, given the existing standards for patentability. Examiners exhibit substantial intrinsic motivation that strongly improves screening quality. We quantify the annual social costs of patent screening at $15.38bn, equivalent to 5% of total private sector R&D in the U.S. and show that reforms limiting the number of rounds of negotiation significantly reduce social costs.

articles.title: Curtailing False News, Amplifying Truth
articles.authors: Sergei Guriev, Emeric Henry, Théo Marquis, Ekaterina Zhuravskaya
articles.abstract: We develop a comprehensive framework to evaluate policy interventions aimed at curbing false news dissemination on social media. Using a randomized experiment on Twitter and X during the 2022 and 2024 U.S. elections, we assess priming for misinformation awareness, fact‐checking, confirmation clicks, and content consideration prompts. Priming proves most effective in reducing false‐news sharing while preserving true news dissemination. We build and structurally estimate a model of sharing, motivated by partisan persuasion, partisan signaling, and reputational concerns. We identify three channels through which policies influence sharing: (i) updating perceived veracity and partisanship of content, (ii) raising salience of reputation, and (iii) increasing engagement costs. Differences in the effects of policies are explained by the salience and cost channels. Content‐neutral priming is best at enhancing salience of reputation at minimal cost and almost as effective as fact‐checking in updating veracity. Salience channel is stronger when users encounter uncontroversially true content.

articles.title: The Random Priority Mechanism Is Uniquely Simple, Efficient, and Fair
articles.abstract: Random Priority is a popular mechanism used to allocate a set of objects to a set of agents without the use of monetary transfers. Random Priority is appealing because it satisfies desirable efficiency, fairness, and incentive properties. Is it the only mechanism with these properties? We answer this long‐standing question in the positive: Random Priority is the unique mechanism that is Pareto efficient, symmetric, and obviously strategy‐proof.

articles.title: Locally Robust Semiparametrically Efficient Bayesian Inference
articles.abstract: We propose a framework for making Bayesian parametric models robust to local misspecification. Suppose in a baseline parametric model, a parameter of interest has an interpretation in an encompassing semiparametric model. Bayesian and maximum likelihood estimators are generally biased under local misspecification. We propose to augment the baseline likelihood by a multiplicative factor that involves scores for the baseline model, the efficient scores for the encompassing semiparametric model, and an auxiliary parameter that has the same dimension as the parameter of interest. We show that the marginal posterior for the parameter of interest in the augmented model is asymptotically normal with mean equal to the semiparametrically efficient estimator and variance equal to the semiparametric efficiency bound. The suggested augmentation robustifies the baseline parametric model to local misspecification, while preserving the appeal of Bayesian inference. We develop an MCMC algorithm for the augmented model and illustrate the approach in applications.

articles.title: Why Do Workers Dislike Inflation? Wage Erosion and Conflict Costs
articles.authors: Joao Guerreiro, Jonathon Hazell, Chen Lian, Christina Patterson
articles.abstract: How costly is inflation to workers? Answers to this question have focused on the path of real wages during inflationary periods. We argue that workers must take costly actions (“conflict”) to have nominal wages catch up with inflation, meaning there are welfare costs even if real wages do not fall as inflation rises. We study a menu‐cost style model, where workers choose whether to engage in conflict with employers to secure a wage increase. We show that, following a rise in inflation, wage catch‐up resulting from more frequent conflict does not raise welfare. Instead, the impact of inflation on worker welfare is determined by what we call “wage erosion”—how inflation would lower real wages if workers' conflict decisions did not respond to inflation. As a result, using observed wage growth to measure worker welfare understates the costs of inflation. We conduct a survey showing that workers are willing to sacrifice around 1.75% of their wages to avoid conflict. Calibrating the model to survey data, we find that incorporating conflict significantly raises the costs of inflation for workers.

articles.title: Causal Inference With Noisy Covariates: Heteroscedastic Measurement Error and Differential Privacy
articles.abstract: We study causal inference with high‐dimensional covariates, observed with various types of heteroscedastic noise. Our main assumption is that the true covariates are low rank, which we empirically evaluate with plots and interpret as approximate repeated measurements. This assumption delivers semiparametric inference on the causal parameter, as precisely as if the true covariates were available. A methodological contribution is to introduce an error‐in‐variable balancing weight for estimation and inference on cross‐sectional causal parameters with heterogeneous effects.

articles.title: Genetic Prediction and Adverse Selection
articles.authors: Eduardo Azevedo, Jonathan P. Beauchamp, Richard Karlsson Linnér
articles.abstract: Recent advances have substantially improved our ability to predict disease risk with genetic data. In response, many countries have banned insurers from using genetic data, despite concerns about adverse selection. This paper measures adverse selection in a market where insurers can underwrite only on nongenetic information while consumers also have access to genetic information. We do so by combining methods from quantitative genetics, selection measures from economic theory, and genetic and electronic health record data on nearly 500,000 individuals in the UK Biobank. We focus on the critical illness insurance market and consider scenarios in which consumers have access to current or expected future genetic prediction technology. We find noticeable levels of selection with current prediction technology, and potentially crippling selection with expected future technology.

articles.title: Sabotage as Industrial Policy
articles.authors: Jin Liu, Martin Rotemberg, Sharon Traiberman
articles.abstract: We characterise sabotage, exemplified by recent US policies concerning China’s semiconductor industry, as trade policy. For some (but not all) goods, completely destroying foreigners’ productivity increases domestic real income by shifting the location of production and improving the terms of trade. The gross benefit of sabotage can be summarised by a few sufficient statistics: trade and demand elasticities and import and production shares. The cost of sabotage is determined by countries’ relative unit labour costs for the sabotaged goods. We find important non-monotonicities: for semiconductors, partially sabotaging foreign production would lower US real income, while comprehensive sabotage would raise it.

articles.title: Government Recommendations and Health Behaviours: Evidence from Breast Cancer Screening Guidelines
articles.authors: Brandyn F Churchill, Emily C Lawler
articles.abstract: We provide novel evidence on how healthcare decision-making responds to government recommendations by examining the 2009 revision to the United States Preventive Services Task Force’s mammography guidelines. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find the revision reduced mammography among women aged 40–49 by 6–10%. We also find spillover effects among women aged 30–39, who became substantially less likely to receive mammogram recommendations or screenings, despite not being the guideline’s target population. Declines were greatest among groups with higher baseline screening rates. We also find evidence of reduced overdiagnosis of early-stage tumors and increased confusion about cancer prevention recommendations.

articles.title: Media Slant is Contagious
articles.authors: Philine Widmer, Clémentine Abed Meraim, Sergio Galletta, Elliott Ash
articles.abstract: This paper examines the diffusion of media slant. We document the influence of Fox News Channel (FNC) on the partisan slant of local newspapers in the U.S. over the years 1995-2008. We measure the political slant of local newspapers by scaling the news article texts to Republicans’ and Democrats’ speeches in Congress. Using channel positioning as an instrument for viewership, we find that higher FNC viewership causes local newspapers to adopt more right-wing slant. The effect emerges gradually, only several years after FNC’s introduction, mirroring the channel’s growing influence on voting behaviour. A main driver of the shift in newspaper slant appears to be a change in local political preferences.

articles.title: Intergroup Contact, Empathy Education, and Refugee-Native Integration in Lebanon
articles.authors: Salma Mousa, Lennard Naumann, Alexandra Scacco
articles.abstract: Intergroup contact interventions often yield limited results in deeply divided societies. We test contact and empathy education in Lebanon, where Syrian refugees comprise a quarter of the population. In a fully cross-randomised field experiment with 887 Lebanese and Syrian youth embedded in a psychosocial support programme, we find that contact has little effect on outgroup attitudes and behaviour, while empathy education consistently improves attitudes for Lebanese youth and behavioural engagement for both. The combined treatment achieves little beyond empathy alone, with no evidence of spillovers to parents (n = 595). In polarised settings, empathy education should precede — or replace — contact.

articles.title: Culture Trumps Class and Place: How the Populist Radical Right Thrives on Sociocultural Conflicts in Western Europe
articles.abstract: Using original survey data from seven Western European countries, this article investigates which social conflicts populist radical right parties (PRRPs) represent. Methodologically, it innovates by measuring individuals’ positions within conflicts combined with the importance they attach to them, capturing both attitudinal alignment and salience. The analysis tests whether traditional cleavages or new conflicts related to globalisation and cultural value change better explain PRRP voting. Findings show that PRRPs predominantly represent new conflicts – individuals opposing cosmopolitanism, LGBTQ+ rights and environmental sustainability – rather than class or territorial divides. While socio-structural traits such as being a production worker or rural resident predict PRRP voting, supporting these groups does not. This decoupling of structure and conflict positions suggests working-class and rural voters are motivated more by culturally reframed grievances than by class- or place-based solidarities. These results highlight the weak link between classic cleavages and PRRP voting, underscoring the centrality of cultural demarcation in today’s political conflict.

articles.title: Why Northern Ireland’s Institutions Need Reform
articles.authors: Sean Haughey, Jon Tonge, Ben Rosher
articles.abstract: In a previous volume of this journal, scholars of consociational power-sharing counselled against reform of Northern Ireland’s power-sharing institutions. Since then, repeated episodes of collapse and dysfunction have necessitated reconsideration of the case for institutional reform. This article argues that a sensible case now exists for reforms to enhance the stability and functionality of Northern Ireland’s consociation. Situating its analysis within broader debates on the evolution of consociational systems, it draws on elite political discourse and original public opinion data (N = 2,034) to assess support for reform and to consider associated trade-offs. We show that changing electoral and ethnonational dynamics have occasioned shifts in elite political attitudes to reform, and highlight public appetite for reform, including in relation to one of the consociation’s most powerful vetoes. Sustainable reform, the article concludes, will be most feasible when elite receptivity to change, civic involvement and (subtle) external support converge.

articles.title: Coerced Voluntariness: Parliamentary Narratives on Return Migration in Germany and Turkey
articles.abstract: International frameworks treat return migration as either voluntary or forced. This article challenges that binary through a computational corpus analysis of two entangled parliaments: 4597 German Bundestag protocols (1949 to 2025, migration analysis from 1970) and 966 Turkish Grand National Assembly protocols (since 2011). In the Bundestag, voluntariness language dominates while coercion oscillates in two waves, peaking in 1994 and 2024. In governing‐party speech the two operate as complementary governance technologies rather than opposites, a pattern termed coerced voluntariness for the German case. A six‐category narrative analysis finds burden ranked first in both parliaments, but the Turkish corpus shows a distinct fraternity‐to‐burden reversal after 2016. Despite documented institutional transfer, the two parliaments converge on burden yet diverge on securitisation: the Bundestag moves towards ethno‐nationalist framing while the Turkish security share stays low and stable. Institutional transfer, the evidence shows, is not matched by discursive convergence.

articles.title: Relational Dynamics and Financial Preparedness for Old Age Among Immigrant Spouses in South Korea: Focusing on Gender Differences
articles.abstract: This study examines how spousal satisfaction and social relations are associated with financial preparedness for old age among marriage‐based immigrants in South Korea, with attention to gender differences. Drawing on nationally representative data from the 2021 National Survey of Multicultural Families and gender‐stratified survey‐weighted regression models, we assess associations between relational resources and perceived preparedness. The findings show that spousal satisfaction and social relations are positively associated with preparedness for both women and men, though the patterns differ. For women, preparedness is linked with both marital and broader social ties, and the association with social relations is stronger at lower levels of spousal satisfaction. For men, preparedness is more strongly associated with spousal satisfaction, with social relations playing a weaker role. These results are interpreted through a social capital perspective, highlighting preparedness as relationally embedded. By analysing both male and female immigrant spouses—an often overlooked population—this study contributes to the growing literature on aging, relational dynamics and migrant integration in East Asia, and underscores the importance of gender‐sensitive perspectives in both research and policy.

articles.title: Friendship in World Politics: George Padmore, Nancy Cunard, and Dorothy Pizer at the End of Empire
articles.abstract: Abstracts This article develops an historical account of friendship as a political relation central to the twentieth-century project of decolonization through an analysis of the writings and political relationships of Trinidadian Pan-African intellectual-activist George Padmore. Towards the end of his life, Padmore thanked “selected allies” and “friends” for their anti-racist and anti-colonial agitation. He conceptualized a political relation of friendship between colonized and colonizer as a potential aid to ending imperial and racialized subordination and domination. Drawing on archival sources, I recover Padmore’s concept of friendship together with its practice by two White women allies: Anglo-American writer Nancy Cunard and English stenographer Dorothy Pizer. Friendship emerges from the situated theorizing and practice of these three intellectual-activists as an always aspirational, potentially transformative, yet inherently asymmetrical political relation. Grounded in difference, anti-colonial friendship was a political practice that unsettled racial hierarchies in the everyday and aimed ultimately to end empire.

articles.title: Populism and the Politics of Aid Classification: Evidence from the OECD Development Assistance Committee
articles.authors: Nicolas Bau, Simone Dietrich, Katharina Fleiner, Alice Iannantuoni
articles.abstract: Abstracts Populist leaders increasingly criticize global governance systems, portraying them as elitist and threatening national sovereignty. While research has explored how populism affects international organizations, less is known about how a rise in populism in donor countries affects engagement with standards in international development cooperation. This research note argues that populism affects how donors classify and present foreign aid projects. Focusing on the OECD’s Development Assistance Committee (DAC), we theorize a mechanism of classification avoidance, whereby bureaucrats anticipate political scrutiny from populists and reduce the use of policy markers that signal alignment with global priorities. Using project-level data on aid activities from 1998 to 2022, we show that increases in anti-elitism in donor legislatures are associated with declines in the share of aid classified as targeting DAC priority areas, alongside stable project screening practices and some but more limited sectoral reallocation. While we do not directly observe bureaucratic decision-making, the empirical patterns are broadly more consistent with anticipatory bureaucratic adaptation than with alternative accounts of policy change. Our paper highlights how domestic political dynamics shape engagement with international standards through bureaucratic practices.

articles.title: From Domestic Contestation to Alpha Male Foreign Policy: Phantasies of Masculinity and the US Self
articles.authors: Veronica Barfucci, Deborah Faudoa Rodríguez, C Nicolai L Gellwitzki
articles.abstract: Abstracts How does masculinity inform the 2024 US presidential election and subsequent US foreign policy? To address this question, we develop the concept of phantasy of masculinity, an affectively charged imaginary that links normalized gender discourses with the narrative reconstruction of Self and Other(s), and that becomes increasingly regressive along a spectrum of intensification towards hypermasculinity. Analyzing official speeches and the media discourse surrounding the 2024 US presidential election campaign and the first year of foreign policy in the second Trump administration, we show that phantasies of masculinity Othering domestic political rivals were central to narrative contestation for both Republicans and Democrats. We further argue that US foreign policy is regressing towards hypermasculinity, in an affectively driven yet ultimately futile attempt to restore ontological security under conditions of perceived crisis. The article makes two contributions to International Relations (IR) scholarship. First, it develops the concept of phantasy of masculinity as a framework for analyzing the psychological and affective dimensions of masculinity. Second, it offers an explanation for seemingly “irrational” US foreign policy under Trump. We conclude by calling for closer integration of feminist IR and Ontological Security Studies to better understand geopolitical implications of gendered insecurities in an uncertain era.

articles.title: Donor Influence at the African Development Bank
articles.abstract: Major powers have prized influence in Africa throughout history. This paper investigates sway over Africa’s foremost international financial institution: the African Development Bank (AfDB). We focus on the two largest nonregional shareholders, the United States and Japan. Analyzing panel data of AfDB loans from 1991 to 2021, we find that increases in Japanese bilateral aid as well as voting with Japan at the United Nations are associated with larger AfDB commitments. We do not uncover similarly convincing evidence of US influence at the AfDB. Qualitative evidence suggests that unlike the United States, Japan’s imperial past and lack of historical ties with Africa encourage a quiet yet persuasive engagement with the institution, which furthers the country’s economic and political aims on the continent. Our results advance the view that governments can pursue their self-interests through international institutions and that they may be particularly successful when they do so subtly.

articles.title: Friending or Blocking? U.S. Public Attitudes toward Restricting Foreign Social Media Apps
articles.authors: Ka Zeng, Damian Raess, Paul Musgrave
articles.abstract: What influences U.S. public support for bans of foreign social media applications? In particular, how do concerns about national security, economic opportunities and threats (such as industrial espionage), reciprocal market access, and the policies and traits of an app influence individual support for banning? We address these questions through a conjoint experiment conducted in November 2024 (N = 1,494). Respondents weighed security threats (such as risks to military interests) and economic interests (including job creation and reciprocal market access) heavily. Concerns about social media platforms themselves, such as strong data privacy protection and content moderation, also mattered, but to a lesser extent. A recontact survey conducted in spring 2025, after President Trump’s decision to reverse the January 2025 TikTok ban, shows stability over time. Overall, our findings reveal a surprisingly strong and stable consensus about what factors promote support for bans—with TikTok-like features arousing opposition among the American public. Nuanced differences do emerge: Republicans and Democrats differ over content moderation policies, while TikTok users and nonusers diverge regarding security threats and owners’ ties to governments. Our findings underscore the importance of the geopolitical and economic implications of foreign apps as well as how consumer experiences influence threat perceptions.

articles.title: International scientific collaboration and political protest
articles.authors: Nils B Weidmann, Mina Rulis, Tore Wig
articles.abstract: Universities as the main institutions of higher education are often assumed to be driving forces of democratization and political liberalization. In autocratic countries, political protest is one of the few ways by which political authority can be challenged, and research has shown that universities often constitute focal points for these protests. However, which universities are particularly likely to see protest? In this paper, we focus on international scientific collaboration. We argue that academic collaboration with universities abroad can facilitate the exchange of information and ideas that challenge autocratic rule. We test our expectations in a preregistered disaggregated study, combining data on academic institutions in autocracies, large publication databases and protest event data. Our findings show that the presence of institutions with a high degree of international scientific collaboration is associated with more protest at a location. However, we find no evidence for our expectation that collaboration with democracies, or in particular disciplines (social sciences), matters more. Overall, our results suggest that beyond the impact on research itself, international academic collaboration can have important political implications in nondemocratic environments.

Beyond redlining: Gentrification, displacement, disadvantages, and exclusivity predict urban environmental and health inequities
articles.authors: Idowu Ajibade, Kevan B. Moffett, Jason Maxfield, Kate Gregory, Axcelle Bell, Jackson Voelkel, Todd Rosenstiel, Aaron R. Ramirez
articles.abstract: This study investigated environmental justice by developing and comparing four contemporary urban segregation typologies (persistent exclusivity, persistent disadvantage, recent gentrification, and recent displacement-hosting) with historical Homeowners’ Loan Corporation (HOLC) zones and 104 variables spanning the natural and built environments, pollution, environmental hazards, health, and disability. We applied principal component analysis to the 2010 and 2020 American Community Survey and the US Census data to derive neighborhood typology indices for 342 tracts in Portland, Oregon. Using Spearman’s correlation and end-member comparisons, we assessed relationships among the typologies, HOLC zones, and environmental and health outcomes. HOLC zones predicted persistently exclusive areas in the urban core but not current injustices elsewhere. Persistently exclusive neighborhoods, both within and outside HOLC zones, had more tree canopy, less dense development, lower disaster risks, better preventive care, and fewer diseases than other areas, but more air pollution exposure. Recently gentrified areas had more transit and community resources but worse heat exposure, pollution, and impervious surface coverage and aligned strongly with HOLC C and D zones. Recent displacement-hosting neighborhoods were cleaner and greener but lack transit and community resources, while exhibiting weak health outcomes. Persistently disadvantaged areas, often outside HOLC zones, faced the most severe conditions, including minimal access to nature, aging infrastructure, the highest pollution and hazard exposure, and the worst health outcomes and disability rates. Our study offers insights into the spatial mechanisms of urban inequities and well-being, underscoring the need to look beyond redlining to fully understand and address today’s social and environmental injustices.

articles.title: Housing tenure, climate resilience, and ecological segregation
articles.authors: Natalie M. Gulsrud, Oriol Garcia-Antúnez, Anton S. Olafsson, Marina Bergen Jensen
articles.abstract: A key challenge to ensuring no one is left behind in the green transition lies in the persistent segregation of urban populations and the unequal distribution of environmental costs and benefits. Residential segregation has long reinforced socioeconomic and racialized disparities, and climate change introduces new dimensions to these injustices as adaptation policies increasingly shift financial and environmental burdens onto marginalized communities. While housing plays a central role in shaping exposure and resilience, the role of housing tenure—especially ownership arrangements beyond market logic—has received limited attention in just green transitions research. This study addresses this gap through a political ecology approach, combining spatial and policy analysis to examine the origins, distribution, and impacts of climate adaptation costs within Copenhagen’s not-for-profit housing sector. Focusing on Hørgården, a stigmatized neighborhood targeted by Denmark’s Parallel Society Law, the study shows how one-size-fits-all adaptation policies can inadvertently exacerbate existing urban inequalities. Findings highlight a missing link related to technomanagerialism, revealing how the interaction between housing tenure, segregation, and climate adaptation financing places disproportionate burdens on marginalized communities. The analysis identifies how institutional silos—particularly between technical and social policy domains—obscure structural drivers of inequality and produce uneven resilience outcomes. The paper offers a theoretical contribution by conceptualizing technomanagerialism as a critical yet overlooked mechanism of inequality within not-for-profit housing systems. It extends debates on climate burdens beyond market-based housing to demonstrate how inequalities become embedded even within ostensibly equitable systems, ultimately reinforcing patterns of urban segregation.

articles.title: From past, persisting, and consolidating ecologies of segregation to ecologies of repair
articles.authors: Isabelle Anguelovski, James J. T. Connolly, Esteve Corbera, David N. Pellow, Fushcia-Ann Hoover, Jacqueline L. Scott, Marccus D. Hendricks, Christopher J. Schell
articles.abstract: Across the United States and Europe, urban and periurban spaces have historically been shaped by land dispossession and enclosure that systematically exclude marginalized, non-White communities from the benefits of society, including access to nature. These dynamics, which have played out and perdured over centuries as part of historic land dispossession and recent green racial capitalism, form the bedrock of contemporary urban segregation and socioecological inequalities. As a result, we see that minoritized and low-wealth groups continue to be deprived of ecological resources and suffer perturbations and loss in urban ecosystem functions and balances. This piece examines the complex relationship between segregation and urban ecologies, drawing on examples from the United States and Europe. We identify five concurrent pathways through which exclusionary land use results in unequal urban ecologies that undermine both social well-being and ecological health. In doing so, we explore how legacies of racial capitalism, colonialism, and segregation create ecologically unbalanced urban landscapes and ecosystems and entangle periurban and rural areas in unequal urbanization. We conclude by advocating for emancipatory and reparative planning practices that confront unequal ecologies and green racial capitalism. These integrate reparations, community-led solutions, equitable green infrastructure, and a radical rethinking of exclusionary socioecological systems.

articles.title: Conceptualizing racial inequalities and injustice in social–ecological systems: A foundation for ecology of segregation
articles.authors: J. Morgan Grove, Steward T. A. Pickett
articles.abstract: Segregation, or social–economic inequity across space, is a widespread phenomenon. What can ecology, with its fundamental concern for spatial heterogeneity, contribute conceptually and practically to issues of segregation? And what can urban ecology learn? The relationships of four established perspectives about environmental inequity and injustice can help answer these questions. All the perspectives acknowledge the social construction of race and similar rankings. Patterns and drivers of segregation originate in extractive capitalism, colonialism, settler colonialism, and unfree labor, and have stimulated a long history of work in environmental justice. A comprehensive framework of environmental justice pattern and processes illustrate the complexity of inequity. The framework begins with a two-dimensional matrix identifying different dimensions of inequity. The conceptual dimensions can be applied to real cases to expose a temporal dynamic. Examples from Baltimore MD, show how the dynamic interactions contribute to larger social–ecological systems that explain the origin and change of segregation in specific places over time. This integration of ecology and broadly social processes is newly emerging. Mechanisms and social–ecological outcomes of segregation based on race are drawn from long-term research in a segregated US metropolitan area. These place-based examples are embedded in broader, globally relevant expressions of segregation that encompass city, suburban, and rural places.

articles.title: Multiple drivers and long-term patterns of the ecology of segregation in Latin America
articles.authors: Elizabeth M. Cook, Jason Sauer, Karin Weil González, Olga Barbosa
articles.abstract: Segregation is a multidimensional phenomenon deeply entwined with historical, social, and ecological contexts. The ecology of segregation framework explores how social norms institutionalize racism, classism, and power dynamics to drive inequitable patterns of environmental benefits and hazards. The ecology of segregation has thus far been applied in the Global North, yet is relevant but not as well studied in the Global South and specifically Latin America. More work is needed to consider how the framework can be applied in other historic, sociocultural, and governance contexts. This paper applies the framework to Valdivia, Chile, illustrating how settler-colonialism, the 1960 9.5 magnitude earthquake, and neoliberal urban policies have shaped Valdivia’s patterns of segregation and ecological outcomes. We explore how social–ecological dynamics act as both press and pulse disturbances that drive inequities, including the displacement of Indigenous Mapuche communities, the spatial restructuring and sprawling development postearthquake, and urban expansion and infill of wetlands influenced by market-oriented governance. Historical colonization entrenched systemic inequalities, while the earthquake altered wetland cover and formalized segregation. More recent land-use policies and urbanization trends further exacerbate disparities, with wealthier neighborhoods gaining greater access to green spaces and environmental amenities. We make the case that the long-term historic patterns and processes have important implications for understanding the current dynamics of—and future trajectories for—environmental justice. The findings call for inclusive urban planning, with community driven bottom–up and top–down approaches and acknowledgment of Indigenous perspectives, to mitigate entrenched inequalities and foster sustainable development.

articles.title: Cognitive control in the presence of a gun
articles.authors: Kyle J. Silva, Brandon J. Schmeichel
articles.abstract: Guns are more prevalent in academic spaces than ever before. Some policy makers have proposed that educators carry guns in schools as a means of self-defense and to protect students, and several states explicitly permit the possession of guns on college campuses. But the psychological consequences of being around guns are relatively unknown. In two preregistered experiments, we tested the hypothesis that being in the presence of a gun undermines cognitive control in a laboratory setting. In both experiments, college students completed a test of attention control [the Squared tasks; A. P. Burgoyne et al. , J. Exp. Psychol. Gen. 152 , 2369–2402 (2023)] in the presence of a (fake) gun or a stapler. In both Experiment 1 ( N = 290) and Experiment 2 ( N = 338) participants in the gun condition scored worse in three of four analyses pertaining to total task performance. These findings suggest that the presence of guns may impair cognitive control and point to heretofore unrecognized potential implications of the “hardening” of academic spaces.

articles.title: Predictors and prevalence of support for white nationalism in the United States
articles.authors: Patrick J. Egan, James Bisbee, Joshua A. Tucker
articles.abstract: White nationalism has become increasingly visible in American public life 1–10 . Yet we lack knowledge of the predictors and prevalence of explicit support for this ideology, as survey research has treated it as a latent construct captured through indirect indicators 11–15 . We introduce and validate a measure that informs respondents of the core tenets of the white nationalist movement and then asks whether they support the movement. Expressed support is distinct from organizational affiliation with the movement, which we do not measure. Here we show with three national surveys of non-Hispanic white adults (conducted from 2021 to 2025) that support for white nationalism is (1) higher among white people encountering personal hardship and local social distress, consistent with strain theories 3,16 ; (2) unrelated to local racial composition or recent demographic change, complicating status threat accounts 4,17,18 ; and (3) elevated among white people with close friendships primarily online, consistent with theories of extremism driven by online mobilization 7,10,19 . Support for white nationalism is more common among white people with lower incomes and education, Republicans and conservatives, and those who are politically disaffected. In our national probability sample, prevalence of support was estimated at 4.9% of white adults, including 13.5% of white men aged 18–29. Support for white nationalism seems to constitute a discrete dimension of white racial attitudes, and many white people who endorse its core ideas are unaware of the label.

articles.title: Shifting sands? The impact of conflict displacement on voting
articles.abstract: Does exposure to conflict displacement amplify support for far-right parties? This study investigates the political consequences of conflict-induced displacement in northern Israel by exploiting a natural experiment arising from government-ordered evacuations during military conflicts. Using a pre-registered survey and a regression discontinuity design based on an exogenous 5 km threshold, I assess changes in retrospective and prospective voting behavior as well as self-reported political ideology. The analysis reveals no evidence that displacement increases far-right support or induces partisan realignment. Rather, evacuees demonstrate a modest rightward shift in ideological self-placement without corresponding changes in voting behavior. This divergence suggests that displacement influences symbolic political positioning without prompting corresponding changes in voting behavior. These patterns unfold against a broader backdrop of political frustration and electoral disengagement that affects both displaced and non-displaced populations. The findings reveal troubling implications for democratic accountability during external conflict: leaders may be shielded from electoral consequences of security failures even as civic engagement deteriorates, challenging models of wartime accountability.

articles.title: Right up my alley: Local radical right success, contextual alignment, and immigration attitudes in Sweden
articles.authors: Stefan Dahlberg, Hilma Lindskog, Henrik Oscarsson
articles.abstract: Electoral success of radical right parties is often argued to normalize previously stigmatized anti-immigration attitudes. Yet, it remains unclear whether such normalization reflects genuine within-individual persuasion or shifts in the local climate of political expression. We address this question by linking highly disaggregated district-level vote shares to individual-level panel survey data from Sweden (2018–2022), a period marked by sustained growth and partial normalization of the Sweden Democrats. Cross-sectional analyses reveal pronounced contextual patterns: Restrictive immigration attitudes are more prevalent in districts with higher local radical right support, particularly among voters who do not support the party, while core supporters remain comparatively stable. However, first-difference panel analyses provide little evidence that changes in local radical right support are associated with attitudinal change. The findings suggest that what appears as normalization in ecological analyses is more consistent with contextual alignment than with rapid persuasion, clarifying the micro-foundations of radical right normalization.

articles.title: The spatial politics of International Climate Finance: A case of India
articles.authors: Soham Banerjee, Dishil Shrimankar, Matthew Paterson
articles.abstract: Do political parties shape where International Climate Funds are allocated? We examine this question in the context of India, where International Climate Funds create opportunities for the central government to leverage externally funded resources to advance domestic political interests. Drawing on a novel geo-coded dataset of project locations from the Kyoto Protocol’s Clean Development Mechanism, we show that projects are more likely to be allocated to constituencies represented by co-partisans of the Prime Minister’s party, and that this effect is strongest in competitive constituencies within states governed by opposition parties, where the central government has the sharpest incentives to build new support. This is surprising because existing literature on the Clean Development Mechanism suggests that decisions on project allocations are depoliticized. By demonstrating otherwise, this article contributes to the literature on International Climate Funds by demonstrating the importance of domestic politics in shaping its distribution.

articles.title: The changing meaning of left-right self-placement in the United Kingdom
articles.abstract: Understanding how voters use the left-right scale is essential, as it is not only related to vote choice but also underpins how political scientists study ideology. This article finds that the way voters use the left-right scale is variable. Using British Election Study Internet Panel data from 2014 to 2024, I find that while economic and cultural values are both related to left-right self-placement, this varies both between individuals and over time. Those on the left of the self-placement scale can best be differentiated from one another by the strength of their economic values. For those on the right, cultural values are more useful in separating between different self-placement levels. Over time, left-right self-placement has become increasingly related to cultural values alongside economic values, driven by movements by people on both sides of the left-right scale. These findings indicate that even within one country, the meanings of ‘left’ and ‘right’ vary.

articles.title: Responsible Algorithmization in the Public Sector: A “Natural Perspective” Based on Ethnographic Research in Regulation, Policing, and Healthcare
articles.authors: Albert Meijer, Lukas Lorenz, Isabelle Donatz‐Fest, Jan‐Luuk Hoff
articles.abstract: Responsible algorithmization refers to the use of algorithms in the public sector while safeguarding public values. Approaches to responsible algorithmization suggested by the EU, OECD, and others depart from a rational perspective and highlight formal structures and procedures. This paper complements this perspective by adding a “natural perspective,” which emphasizes sense‐making and actual practices. This natural perspective is used for a set of ethnographic studies of algorithmization in three domains in the Netherlands: regulation, policing, and healthcare. Our findings show that algorithmization of government organizations is an emergent, political, open, and fragmented process, rather than, as assumed by rational approaches to responsible algorithmization, pre‐structured, neutral, closed, and simple. This means that rational approaches fall short of providing a comprehensive basis for establishing responsible algorithmization. We conclude that not only passive responsibility but also active responsibility for algorithmization in the public sector needs to be addressed to safeguard public values.

articles.title: A Public Values Framework for AI Governance: Evidence From US Federal AI Policymaking
articles.authors: Ogadinma Enwereazu, Kaylyn Jackson Schiff, Tyler Girard, Alexander Wilhelm, Daniel S. Schiff
articles.abstract: Governments at all levels are grappling with AI's implications for public administration. Because federal actions often establish the principles guiding wider governance efforts, this study asks how US federal AI policies reflect—or fail to reflect—core public values. Drawing on a dataset of US federal AI policies from 2020 to 2023, we systematically analyze the risks, harms, and governance strategies employed across government‐issued and enacted policy documents. Specifically, we analyze 120 discrete policy sections or subsections of federal laws and regulations, utilizing the parsing approach of the AI Governance and Regulatory Archive (AGORA), all of which regulate the operation of the government itself rather than private sector behavior. We develop a theoretical and empirical crosswalk linking AI‐related risks and harms to prominent public values. Results indicate that while values such as individual rights, the common good, and accountability are regularly invoked, additional guidance around public values like citizen engagement, workplace standards, and responsiveness may be necessary to prevent public value failure. The study further categorizes governance strategies in AI policy documents into regulatory, service‐based, and informational instruments, and finds that regulatory policies are most likely to engage with public values.

articles.title: Inspired to Serve: Exposure to Moral Models to Enhance Public Service Motivation
articles.authors: Xiaoyu Wang, James L. Perry, Yuming Wang, Dingxiang Chen, Bangcheng Liu
articles.abstract: Public service motivation (PSM) is widely recognized as a predictor of positive outcomes, yet relatively little is known about how it can be deliberately cultivated. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory, the present research investigates whether and how exposure to moral exemplars embedded in public‐sector training enhances PSM. Employing a multi‐method design that combines a recall experiment with a field survey, we find that exposure to uncommon moral exemplars elicits moral elevation, which functions as a replenishment of psychological resources and, in turn, strengthens public employees' PSM. Moreover, this mediating mechanism is moderated by cognitive load, such that public employees experiencing greater cognitive demands derive stronger motivational benefits from moral elevation. By identifying moral elevation as a psychological resource mechanism and cognitive load as a boundary condition, this research opens the “black box” of PSM development. It highlights how training can serve as an institutional platform for delivering specific moral content that cultivates and sustains public employees' motivation to serve.

articles.title: From Civic Tech to DOGE : The Role of Tech Movements in the American Administrative State
articles.abstract: The second Trump administration saw the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a group of outsider technologists given extraordinary power to pursue a massive downsizing of the federal government. They also displaced an alternative approach: the civic tech movement. Civic tech for government applies technology, data, and human‐centered design to improve policy implementation, fueled by prosocial motivation, promising to increase state capacity in a way that centers attention on public service clients. This article explains the origins of civic tech for government in the US setting, its core values, and evolution. The movement grew in prominence and influence from 2014 to 2024, making steady inroads into government but never gaining sufficient power to implement profound change. The conflicting origins, philosophy, and power between civic tech and DOGE offer contrasting visions for how tech can reshape the American administrative state.

articles.title: The Right Key for the Right Lock: How Government Response Methods and Demand Types Affect Citizen Satisfaction
articles.authors: Na Tang, Wenjia Huang, Nana Huang, Mengyao Zhang
articles.abstract: Faced with diverse and complex demands from citizens, the government has consistently sought ways to enhance its ability to respond. Metaphorically, citizens' needs can be viewed as locks, and the government requires keys to unlock them. Artificial intelligence (AI) is an innovative new key offering a fresh paradigm for unlocking the door to high citizen satisfaction. Drawing on government responsiveness theory, this study applies a 2 × 3 between‐subjects survey experiment to explore the impact of government response methods (traditional responses, AI‐enabled responses) and citizen demand types (consultation, complaint/help‐seeking, suggestions) on citizen satisfaction. Findings show that AI‐enabled government responses significantly increase citizen satisfaction compared to traditional approaches. Among demand types, consultation yields the highest satisfaction, while suggestion results in the lowest. Further, the satisfaction level is significantly influenced by the interaction effect between response method and demand type. Perceived fairness mediates the relationship between government responses and citizen satisfaction, with citizen participation experience having a moderating effect. This study offers new insights into increasing citizen satisfaction from the perspective of government responses. It reveals the content‐dependent nature of AI‐enabled government responses, helping the government create unique AI response strategies and enhance digital interaction with citizens.
