articles.title: The “Professional Mortality” Problem in Early City Management: A Study of Organized Denial
articles.abstract: The early city management profession experienced appalling rates of attrition. This problem of “professional mortality” had been clearly recognized by the end of World War I: causes of attrition included threats and violence against managers, intense political interference in managers' work, and interpersonal missteps. Yet the organized management profession and advocates of the manager plan actively ignored threats and were unwilling to respond collectively or officially to political interference; leading scholars recognized but did not publicly discuss common interpersonal problems faced by managers. This silence on the underlying causes of turnover marked an effort to protect the manager plan's viability in the face of growing electoral opposition during the 1920s, placing the interests of the profession above its practicing members. The optimistic, rationalist discourses of advocates, scholars, and professional leaders rested on self‐conscious denial of uncomfortable realities; a full historical accounting may help avoid repeating these mistakes.

articles.title: Elites, Policies and State Reconfiguration: Transforming the French Welfare Regime. By WilliamGenieys and Mohammad‐SaïdDarviche, Cham, Switzerland: Palgrave Macmillan, 2023. 209 pp. $169.99 (hardcover). ISBN: 978‐3‐03‐141581‐4

Routledge Handbook on Crisis, Polycrisis, and Public Administration. By KimMoloney, Gloria J.Billingsley, Bok GyoJeong, PabloSanabria‐Pulido, Tonya E.Thornton, and EricZeemering, New York, New York: Routledge, 2025. 390 pp. $280.00 (hardback) ( eBook $58.39). ISBN: 978‐1‐00‐333363‐0
Voting for Democracy? Testing Political-Cultural Constraints on Democratic Backsliding
articles.abstract: Democratic backsliding continues to pose a clear danger to contemporary democracies. While a growing literature shows that voters often tolerate antidemocratic candidates when partisan or ideological incentives pull in that direction, we know less about whether support for democracy, institutional trust, political tolerance, and other democratic orientations ameliorate such temptations. We address this question with a systematic comparison of six measures of political culture as predictors of electoral resistance to antidemocratic candidates. Using candidate-choice conjoint experiments fielded in three democracies facing backsliding pressures—the United States, Poland, and South Korea—we find that several democratic orientations are associated with greater resistance to antidemocratic candidates. Among them, support for the core institutions and processes of liberal democracy stands out as the most consistent predictor. Its relationship with prodemocratic choice remains meaningful even in “cross-pressured” choices where partisan or ideological incentives pull voters away from the prodemocratic option. These findings suggest that political culture matters for democratic resilience, though some components of it matter much more consistently than others.

articles.title: Attention to the Macroeconomy
articles.authors: Sebastian Link, Andreas Peichl, Oliver Pfäuti, Christopher Roth, Johannes Wohlfart
articles.abstract: We measure which economic topics are top of mind using quarterly German household and firm panels from 2020 to 2024, a period that spans the post-pandemic inflation surge and the subsequent disinflation. With these data, we study potential determinants and consequences of having inflation top of mind. In line with goal-directed attention, the likelihood that inflation is top of mind rises with proxies for its true payoff relevance. At the same time, prior experiences predict whether respondents have inflation and energy prices top of mind conditional on a large set of controls for payoff relevance, and this relationship strengthens when the environment becomes more inflationary. Having inflation top of mind predicts stronger increases in information acquisition and inflation expectations over the shock period. At odds with goal-optimality, having inflation top of mind is associated with expectations further away from multiple ex-ante benchmarks. Finally, both key determinants of having inflation top of mind—payoff relevance and prior experiences—are associated with stronger shifts of expectations away from these benchmarks over the shock period.

articles.title: Stockups, Stockouts, and the Role for Strategic Reserves
articles.authors: Brett Green, Cyrus Mevorach, Curtis R Taylor
articles.abstract: We study how supply disruptions interact with monopoly pricing, inventory management, and consumer stockpiling in a continuous-time model. Preemption incentives—consumers prefer to stock up before a price hike while the firm prefers to hike before consumers stock up—lead to an equilibrium with gradual stockpiling and endogenous uncertainty over the timing of a price hike, which can trigger a run at the disruption onset. Consumer storage introduces welfare losses from randomized pricing, but can also strengthen the firm’s incentive to hold buffer stock. Rationing, price controls, and reserve mandates can each improve welfare, but only strategic government reserves can implement the social optimum.

articles.title: Company Wage Policy in a Low-Wage Labor Market
articles.abstract: We study how firms set wages for their employees when they can legally age-discriminate across workers. We exploit an age-specific minimum wage change in the UK, which raised the minimum applying to workers aged 25 and over, leaving unchanged the minima for younger workers. Using matched employer-employee data on a low-paying sector, we show large, positive wage spillovers on workers aged under 25, which arise within firms from company wage policy. Pay equity norms offer the most parsimonious explanation for the emergence of spillovers. The effects that we document also operate in other low-paying sectors of the UK labor market.

articles.title: Measuring Markets for Network Goods
articles.authors: Leonardo Bursztyn, Matthew Gentzkow, Rafael Jiménez-Durán, Aaron Leonard, Filip Milojević, Christopher Roth
articles.abstract: Market definition is challenging in settings with network effects, where substitution patterns depend on changes in network size. We study these effects in the context of social media. We conduct an incentivized experiment comparing substitution in response to a proposed U.S. TikTok ban, in which all users simultaneously leave the app, with substitution when only a single user deactivates. We find substantially higher valuations of alternative social apps under a collective TikTok ban than under an individual TikTok deactivation. Mechanism evidence shows that both anticipated content-supply shifts and social coordination partly explain the wedge, with the relative importance of each channel varying across platforms. We then show that a collective time limit challenge, where peers jointly reduce TikTok and Instagram use, leads to more time spent on alternative social apps than has been observed in prior individual deactivation experiments. Together, our results suggest that individual-level substitution estimates can be an unreliable guide to market definition for network goods.

articles.title: Machine Learning for Dynamic Incentive Problems
articles.abstract: We present a flexible and scalable computational framework integrating machine learning and optimization theory to solve dynamic adverse selection models with persistent private information and many types. Our approach reformulates the model into a numerically tractable structure that bypasses set-valued dynamic programming; we formally prove that, under verifiable conditions, this relaxation yields the solution to the original problem. The recast problem is solved via a parallelized value function iteration algorithm, where high-dimensional, nonlinear functions are approximated using Gaussian process regression combined with Bayesian active learning. We apply our framework to two previously intractable models: one with persistent hidden information involving up to ten types and another incorporating multiple persistent types and overreporting. Validation against known solutions and rigorous credibility measures confirms accuracy. Allowing overreporting significantly alters long-run contract outcomes, concentrating consumption away from extremes and smoothing utility promises over time.

articles.title: Entry and Profits in an Aging Economy: The Role of Consumer Inertia
articles.abstract: Over the past four decades, the U.S. economy has seen a decline in the share of young firms alongside a rise in the profit share of GDP. This paper explores how population aging contributes to these twin trends through a demand-side channel. The core hypothesis is that younger households exhibit lower consumer inertia—a tendency to stick with previously chosen products—than older households. As demand shifts toward more inertial consumers, entry becomes harder, incumbents raise markups, and market share tilts toward larger firms. To quantify this mechanism, I develop and calibrate a firm dynamics model with overlapping generations of consumers who differ in their degree of inertia. Using detailed micro data, I show that younger households are significantly less inertial. The model implies that population aging accounts for 20%–30% of the observed decline in young firms and rise in profits. Reduced-form evidence across U.S. states and product categories supports the model’s predictions.

articles.title: Demographics, Wealth, and Global Imbalances in the Twenty-First Century
articles.authors: Adrien Auclert, Hannes Malmberg, Frédéric Martenet, Matthew Rognlie
articles.abstract: We use a sufficient statistic approach to quantify the general equilibrium effects of population aging on the returns to wealth, wealth accumulation, and global imbalances. Combining population forecasts with household survey data from 25 countries, we measure the compositional effect of aging: how a changing age distribution affects wealth-to-GDP, holding the age profiles of wealth and labor income fixed. In a baseline overlapping generations model this statistic, in conjunction with cross-sectional information and two standard macro parameters, pins down general equilibrium outcomes. Since the compositional effect is positive, large, and heterogeneous across countries, our model predicts that population aging will lower returns to wealth, increase wealth-to-GDP ratios, and widen global imbalances through the twenty-first century. These conclusions extend to a richer model in which bequests, individual savings, and the tax-and-transfer system all respond to demographic change.

articles.title: The End of Oil
articles.abstract: Even as global oil demand has increased in recent years, it is plausible to envision scenarios in which clean energy technologies or climate policies drive demand to essentially zero by the century’s end. This paper asks what such a demand decline, when anticipated, might mean for global oil supply. One possibility is a “green paradox”: producers accelerate extraction. However, because extraction requires durable capital investments, the opposite may occur: producers reduce their investment rate, decreasing extraction. To evaluate the relative strengths of these opposing mechanisms, I develop a model of global oil supply that incorporates both, among other industry features. For model inputs with the strongest empirical support, both effects are modest, with disinvestment typically outweighing the green paradox. In order for the green paradox to substantially increase cumulative global oil extraction, investments must have short time horizons, and producers’ discount rates must be less than 4% real.

articles.title: From Micro to Macro in an Equilibrium Diffusion Model
articles.authors: Wyatt Brooks, Kevin Donovan, Terence R. Johnson
articles.abstract: We quantify the benefits of better firm-to-firm matching in an aggregate diffusion model where individuals acquire profitable knowledge from others. We estimate the model using a small-scale program in Kenya that creates new opportunities for firm managers to interact. Aggregate gains from the program depend on the relative importance of meeting a high-knowledge firm versus learning within that meeting. We show how moments from the intervention identify these parameters, demonstrating how easily estimated moments beyond the average treatment effect inform at-scale gains. We provide sufficient conditions extending the identification procedure to a broader class of experiments and aggregate diffusion models.

articles.title: Transaction Costs and the Gains from Trade in Water Markets
articles.abstract: Surface water in California is scarce and tightly managed, yet little is traded through a market. This paper studies transaction costs in the existing wholesale water market and estimates the benefits of reducing them. I develop an empirical framework that uses transactions among water districts to analyze welfare, decomposing prices into demand and transaction costs and simulating a market with only physical frictions. Transaction costs are large: median variable costs are 54% of the price, and fixed costs deter many districts from participating. Eliminating them produces gains of several hundred million dollars per year, or 1-3% of statewide water expenditures.

articles.title: Insurance Choice with Non-Monetary Plan Attributes: Limited Consideration in Medicare Part D
articles.abstract: I propose a model of insurance demand where non-monetary attributes determine which plans an individual considers, and monetary attributes determine an individual's expected utility. This approach reconciles the classic view of insurance as purely financial with the empirical finding that choice is driven by additional attributes. I estimate the model using Medicare Part D data, allowing for unobserved heterogeneity in consideration and preferences. I find the former plays a crucial role: more than 90% of individuals consider 5 or fewer plans, approximately lO°lo of the menu. Additionally, estimates of risk preferences are comparable to existing studies of similar stakes.

articles.title: Social Ties and Fiscal Transfers in a Regional Economy: A Quantitative Spatial Analysis
articles.authors: Yuwan Duan, Yatang Lin, Yi Lu
articles.abstract: Many governments use fiscal transfers to reduce regional inequality, yet discretionary allocation may also depend on informal communication among officials. We examine this mechanism in a large central-to-provincial transfer system, using policymakers’ shared workplace, alumni, and hometown backgrounds to measure social ties. Exploiting ministerial turnover and controlling for provincial leadership, we find that prior workplace ties significantly increase transfers. We then embed these estimates in a quantitative spatial model with trade, migration, input-output linkages, and fiscal-productivity effects. Social ties redirect resources toward richer provinces with stronger fundamentals, raising welfare and output while weakening redistribution. Under egalitarian weights, however, removing ties improves welfare.

articles.title: Scientific Talent Leaks Out of Funding Gaps
articles.authors: Wei Yang Tham, Joseph Staudt, Elisabeth Ruth Perlman, Stephanie D. Cheng
articles.abstract: Federal research funding is a key input into scientific work, but funding streams can be disrupted. We study how delays in renewed NIH research grants affect lab personnel’s careers, linking grant records to university payroll, tax, Census, and publication data. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that interruptions of at least 30 days increase nonemployment among personnel in labs supported by a single NIH R01 grant by 3 percentage points, or 40%. Among those who remain employed in the US, earnings decrease by 20%. The results show that short funding gaps can alter career trajectories, especially for trainees.

articles.title: Return to Office and the Tenure Distribution
articles.authors: David Van Dijcke, Florian Gunsilius, Austin Wright
articles.abstract: Debates over return-to-office mandates have intensified since the COVID-19 pandemic ended, though their economic implications remain poorly understood. Using large-scale resume data, we analyze how these policies affect employee tenure and seniority at three large U.S. tech companies: Microsoft, SpaceX, and Apple. Employing a distributional synthetic controls framework, we estimate a reduction in tenure and seniority at firms returning to the office. We extend the framework with a functional bootstrap procedure and prove its validity for constructing uniform confidence bands. Return-to-office mandates appear to drive senior employees away, posing a risk to firm productivity and innovation.

articles.title: Job Loss, Unemployment Insurance, and Health: Evidence from Brazil
articles.authors: Guilherme Amorim, Diogo G. C. Britto, Alexandre Fonseca, Breno Sampaio
articles.abstract: We study the health impacts of job loss and unemployment insurance (UI) among Brazilian workers, using unique administrative data linking employment, hospitalizations, health insurance, and mortality records over 17 years. Leveraging mass layoffs for identification, we find that job loss raises hospitalization (+33%) and mortality (+23%) risks for men, with no significant effects for women. Impacts are pervasive across age, income, and education levels, with children of male workers also affected. External causes related to risky behavior and violence victimization explain half the effects. Using a regression discontinuity design, we show that UI partially mitigates health risks, suggesting that these are partially explained by income losses.

articles.title: Estimating the Macroeconomic Effects of Oil Supply News
articles.abstract: We show that structural oil-market shocks identified in prominent SVAR models, as well as high-frequency oil price changes around OPEC announcements, are predictable, indicating informational deficiencies in standard oil-market VARs and contamination of commonly used instrumental variables. We resolve these identification problems for oil supply news shocks by augmenting the econometrician’s information set with financial indicators, yielding markedly different results: the shocks induce a sharper short-run output contraction, are less inflationary, contribute less to oil price variation, exhibit greater stability over time, and account for a substantial share of S&P 500 volatility.

articles.title: The Intergenerational Transmission of Employers and the Earnings of Young Workers
articles.abstract: This paper investigates how parental connections to firms shape early-career earnings. I use employer-employee linked data to study one important type of connection: jobs obtained at a parent’s employer. Twenty-nine percent of individuals work for a parent’s employer at least once by age 30. Exploiting transitory, firm-specific fluctuations in hiring conditions at the parent’s employer, I estimate that working for a parent’s employer increases initial earnings by 24 percent, primarily by providing access to higher-paying firms. Individuals with higher-earning parents are more likely to work for a parent’s employer and experience larger earnings gains when they do. Consequently, the elasticity of initial earnings with respect to parental earnings would be 12 percent lower if no one found a job through these connections. The findings suggest that connections to firms through one’s social network may be an important determinant of intergenerational mobility.

articles.title: Gender and Electoral Incentives: Evidence from COVID-19 Response
articles.abstract: This paper provides new evidence on why men and women leaders make different choices. Exploiting Brazilian close elections, we show that female mayors responded differently to the COVID-19 crisis over the year 2020. Female mayors were less likely to close non-essential businesses early in the pandemic and female-led municipalities experienced higher mortality, while the reverse was true later on. We show that these findings can be rationalized by a simple political agency model in which politicians seek re-election and voters are gender biased. Consistent with this interpretation, the gender differences we find are driven exclusively by mayors facing re-election.

articles.title: Losing Political Representation
articles.authors: Timo Wochner, Aaron Günther, Niklas Potrafke, Felix Rösel
articles.abstract: What are the consequences of losing political representation in a democracy? A reform of Germany’s mixed electoral system left more than 7 million citizens in 23 constituencies without a directly elected representative after the 2025 national election. Which and how many constituencies were affected was unpredictable and quasi-random. We show that losing geographical representation reduces citizens’ satisfaction with democracy. Moreover, discontent is independent of party preferences and spreads through social networks, reducing democratic satisfaction even among individuals who were unaffected or unaware of the reform’s outcome. We conclude that political representation is a cornerstone of democracy.

articles.title: Gender Discrimination in Access to Capital: A Field Experiment in Ethiopia
articles.authors: Ketki Sheth, Shanthi Manian, Shibiru Ayalew
articles.abstract: We test whether loan officers discriminate against female business owners in capital decisions affecting real businesses in an Ethiopian business plan competition. Randomizing owner gender across 3,696 evaluations, by 84 loan officers, for 916 businesses, we find no effect on prize scores or consideration for a loan. Incentivized beliefs about future performance did not differ by gender, ruling out statistical and taste-based discrimination. Machine learning predictions of future business performance show that loan officers beliefs were accurate. Gender does not meaningfully improve predictions, implying no trade-off between gender equity and effective capital allocation.

articles.title: Curricular-credential decoupling: how schools respond to college and career readiness policy
articles.authors: Matt S Giani, Madison E Andrews, Tasneem Sultana, Fortunato N Medrano
articles.abstract: This study examines schools’ college and career readiness (CCR) policy responses through the lens of decoupling. We investigate how high schools have jointly implemented career and technical education (CTE) and industry-based certifications (IBCs), and whether there is evidence of curricular-credential decoupling via misalignment between the subject areas of students’ CTE coursework and IBC completion. Descriptive analyses of Texas’s statewide longitudinal dataset (n = 2,119,750) demonstrate the rapid rise in certification rates combined with minimal change in CTE course-taking patterns and a concomitant decline in the rate of CTE-IBC alignment, suggesting schools may be using IBCs as a superficial way to meet CCR requirements. Regression analyses show modest relationships between student characteristics and IBC receipt and CTE-IBC misalignment, while schools explain a substantial proportion of variation. We develop a typology based on these school-level rates, which may be a useful tool for understanding schools’ strategies for CCR implementation across state policy contexts. By comparing school characteristics across typology categories, we highlight factors that may contribute to misalignment and inform policy.

Occupational hazard and political segregation in the US labor market
articles.abstract: The tendency for liberals and conservatives to cluster in different occupations significantly impacts society, yet the factors that contribute to this type of segregation remain incompletely understood. Bridging research from cultural and cognitive psychology, I develop a theory describing how occupational environments can shape people’s political ideologies, thereby contributing to political segregation in the labor market. Specifically, I argue that the more hazardous an occupation is, the more likely it is to have a higher concentration of conservative workers because dangerous work environments can socialize people to prefer order and stability. Using data from the Occupation Information Network, General Social Survey, and Bureau of Labor Statistics, I find that hazardous occupations tend to have higher concentrations of conservative workers, even after controlling for several alternative explanations. Further, using longitudinal data from the Youth-Parent Socialization Panel Study, I find that individuals employed in hazardous occupations tended to become more conservative over time relative to their peers in safer occupations. These findings suggest that liberals and conservatives may not only be sorting into different occupations; rather, certain occupational environments may contribute to political segregation in the labor market by shaping workers’ political views.

Internal and International Migration of Scholars in Times of Conflict: The Case of Ukraine, 2009‐2022
articles.abstract: Current migration theories occasionally ignore the potentially negative aspects of scholarly migration as a form of high‐skilled migration, largely viewing it in a positive light. Yet scholarly migration is not always a tale of freedom and innovation, as the labels “researchers at risk” and “scientists in exile” demonstrate. We document the problematic aspects of conflict‐related scholarly migration among researchers with Ukraine‐affiliated publication histories from 2009 to 2022. We primarily draw on OpenAlex bibliometric records to reconstruct affiliation‐based migration histories and aggregate them to Ukraine's first‐level administrative regions. Results suggest that after 2014 there was substantial internal and international out‐migration from the occupied Eastern Ukrainian regions as well as the annexed Crimean peninsula, with over 50 per 1,000 scholars leaving the Eastern regions to both internal and international destinations and over 100 per 1,000 scholars out‐migrating from Crimea to international destinations in the first three years after the start of the conflict in 2014. These results show how armed conflict can be associated with a reorganization of national science systems by changing where researchers work and publish, thereby calling into question accounts that treat scholarly mobility primarily as voluntary high‐skilled migration.

articles.title: How Political Events Become Demographic: Toward a Cumulative Demography of Conflict and Violence
articles.authors: Mathis Ebbinghaus, Liliana Andriano, Patrick Heuveline
articles.abstract: Political conflict and violence shape the core demographic processes of mortality, migration, and fertility, while also influencing union formation, health, and kinship networks. Existing studies have often asked whether conflict is positively or negatively associated with demographic outcomes, yet findings remain strikingly mixed. This reflects the heterogeneous nature of conflict and violence themselves, the institutional and social contexts in which they occur, and the multiple, interacting processes through which they influence demographic outcomes. To advance a cumulative research program for conflict demography, we identify three priorities. First, researchers should distinguish exposure to conflict and violence from the extent to which individuals are affected by them and take seriously the processes of meaning‐making through which conflict events acquire demographic significance. Second, researchers should identify a limited set of generalizable social mechanisms that connect conflict and violence to demographic outcomes, recognizing that the same mechanism can produce different empirical results in different contexts. Third, researchers should develop macro‐level analyses of conflict‐affected populations because changes in population size, composition, and distribution are population‐level processes that cannot be derived solely from micro‐level mechanisms. The articles in this issue exemplify these three priorities and together outline a methodologically plural program for a cumulative conflict demography.

Partisans misperceive and are influenced by dynamic norms
articles.authors: Trystan Loustau, Ashley Fabrizio, Liane Young, Jordan Wylie, Stylianos Syropoulos
articles.abstract: Perceptions of social norms, and how those norms change over time, play a central role in shaping how people understand and respond to political divides. We developed and iteratively refined dynamic‐norm messages about bipartisan attitude change to reduce divisive outparty perceptions and attitudes in a US context. We first identified real‐world issues that gained support over time among both Democrats and Republicans and were judged as believable. Study 1 documented systematic misperceptions of attitude change across a range of social issues and linked these misperceptions to colder outparty feelings. We then tested intervention messages that adapted standard static‐norm templates with the addition of information about change over time (dynamic norm; Study 2). This intervention increased expectations of future common ground but did not reliably improve downstream outparty attitudes. Next, we tested a refined intervention message that isolated dynamic norm information (Study 3). The refined dynamic norm message increased expected common ground and expected future feelings of belonging among the outparty and was associated with small but reliable increases in outparty warmth and positive outparty impressions relative to control. These results suggest that emphasizing trajectories of public opinion without highlighting current partisan gaps may be a useful strategy for reducing polarization.

articles.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Open‐Source LLMs for Automated Analysis of Multilingual Consultation Feedback: A Swiss Case Study
articles.abstract: Public consultations are a cornerstone of democratic policymaking, yet the sheer volume and heterogeneity of submissions often overwhelm traditional analysis. Emerging large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for making sense of such data, but their performance in contexts with high linguistic and technical diversity remains underexplored. In this research note, we present a case‐based demonstration rather than a generalizable evaluation, assessing an open‐source LLM (Gemma3:27b) and a proprietary LLM (GPT‐5‐mini) for analyzing stakeholder inputs from three Swiss pre‐parliamentary consultations. The coexistence of multiple languages and varying technical complexity in submissions creates uniquely challenging datasets, providing a rigorous test for automated tools. We benchmark the model against official administrative reports, assessing accuracy and completeness. Results show the open‐source model performs excellently in straightforward consultations, achieving a mean accuracy of 90%, but encounters difficulties in retrieving the substantive content (overall completeness: 70%). Comparatively, the proprietary model obtains better results than the open‐source one in these two settings. Overall, LLMs can streamline analysis and enhance interpretive capacity, complementing (but not replacing) human expertise. The study highlights both the potential and limits of algorithmic support for participatory governance in linguistically and technically diverse environments.

articles.title: From Antagonistic Talk to Cooperative Acts: The Effect of Polarization Cues on Newspaper Audiences
articles.abstract: Do media depictions of a ‘polarized society’ merely describe division or actually deepen it? We report two laboratory experiments in Germany (Study1 $$N=302$$ ; Study2 $$N=295$$ ). After reading authentic newspaper articles in which brief polarization cues were experimentally included versus omitted, participants (i) completed standard affective- and ideological-polarization measures and (ii) played incentivized Dictator, Ultimatum, and Trust Games with ideological out-group partners. Polarization cues increased both affective polarization and ideological extremity. Behavioral responses, however, were mixed. In the Dictator Game, where the recipient cannot respond, treated participants shared less with the out-group. In the Trust Game, characterized by mutual dependence and potential efficiency gains, treated participants sent more to out-group partners. Ultimatum behavior, where interdependence is partial, showed weaker and less consistent shifts. Taken together, polarization cues reliably heighten perceived division but do not uniformly translate into behavioral antagonism: even after cues that increase self-reported polarization, participants can still cooperate with ideological opponents when cooperation is perceived as mutually beneficial.

articles.title: The Limits of Incumbent Blame Games in Times of Crisis: Experimental Evidence from Electoral Autocracy
articles.abstract: This study investigates how blame-attributing crisis frames influence support for incumbents in an electoral authoritarian context, focusing on Türkiye. It asks how, to what extent, and under what conditions incumbents’ blame frames shape public attitudes toward the government. The study examines four crisis types (i.e., global warming , earthquake , economic collapse , and pandemic ) and compares the effects of religious , conspiratorial , and scientific framing across these contexts. Drawing on original data from seven pre-survey focus groups and a nationwide face-to-face survey experiment with 3,562 respondents, the findings indicate that the independent effects of blame frames are generally limited. However, the effectiveness of religion-based blame framing is highly context dependent. Compared with climate and economic crises, its estimated effects are more favorable in crises characterized by high uncertainty and relatively low perceived governmental responsibility, such as earthquake and pandemic. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of blame attribution is conditioned by the nature of the crisis itself. The study contributes to research on crisis framing, political accountability, and authoritarian durability.

articles.title: Left Behind or Left In? Party Ideology and the Gender Gap in Candidate Persistence
Credible Prejudice? When and Why Mainstream Party Adoption of Far-Right Rhetoric Weakens Anti-Prejudice Norms
articles.abstract: This article examines whether mainstream political parties adopt prejudiced rhetoric from the far right and how such shifts shape anti-prejudice norms. Building on existing work, I argue that mainstream parties are particularly influential in weakening anti-prejudice norms because they possess greater normative credibility and legitimacy than far-right parties. Empirically, the article combines cross-national observational evidence with two preregistered survey experiments in Germany and Denmark. Using parliamentary speeches from six European countries between 1994 and 2022, I document rising mainstream party anti-Muslim rhetoric and its association with weaker norms against holding far-right views. The experiments provide causal evidence for the argument. In Germany, exposure to prejudiced rhetoric weakens anti-prejudice norms, but only when voiced by mainstream parties, rather than far right parties, likely due to their normative credibility and legitimacy. In Denmark, comparable effects are absent, consistent with decades of mainstream accommodation having already normalized such rhetoric. The experimental results also show that rhetoric targeting Muslims weakens anti-prejudice norms toward out-groups more broadly, suggesting spillover effects. These findings have important implications for future scholarship: when mainstream parties adopt prejudiced rhetoric from the far right, they affect not only electoral politics, but also the broader social norm environment.

articles.title: Do Political Discussion Partners Share Policy Priorities and Policy Frames?
articles.authors: Matthew T. Pietryka, Amber E. Boydstun, Taylor N. Carlson
articles.abstract: To understand politics, people often rely on political discussion. Among the many ways that discussion may shape political perceptions, one possible mechanism is by promoting a shared sense of priorities— which issues are important. A second mechanism is by framing how people think about important issues. We examine these potential mechanisms by answering the descriptive question: Do policy priorities and policy frames tend to co-occur within political discussion networks? We answer this question by reanalyzing the 1996 Indianapolis-St. Louis Study in which participants—and their discussion partners—described the most important problem facing the United States in their own words. We show that the modal outcome is for people to hold both different priorities and different frames than their discussion partners. This finding stands in contrast to network scholarship suggesting that homophily is so often the norm. Yet we also show that people disproportionately share the same policy priorities as their discussion partners, and adopt the same frames in thinking about policy topics, especially when their policy priorities match. This finding suggests that some policy priorities are so embedded in certain frames of thinking that the topic and frame stay linked even as the topic may diffuse through a social network.

articles.title: Turning Hazard Models Inside Out
articles.authors: David Melamed, Jack G. R. Wippell, Eric W. Schoon, Ronald L. Breiger
articles.abstract: Regression Inside Out (RIO) describes a set of related methods based on a decomposition of regression coefficients by individual cases. In this article, we offer three important extensions of RIO: 1) we generalize RIO to any model for which linear predictors are estimated; 2) we introduce an adapted bootstrap approach for determining whether case-level contributions differ from the baseline average contribution for cases; and 3) we describe how RIO is related to model diagnostics, particularly DFBETA. To illustrate the value added of these extensions, we apply RIO to a published example of the Cox proportional hazard model exploring factors associated with democratic durability.

The Evolution of Committee Agenda Control in the Antebellum U.S. House of Representatives
articles.authors: John Baughman, Chris Den Hartog, Craig Goodman
articles.abstract: Gatekeeping is viewed as an essential element of committee power in the U.S. Congress, but its emergence is not well understood. The House of Representatives moved to a system of standing committees by 1825. We investigated whether that move gave committees gatekeeping power prior to the Civil War or layered committees atop the earlier Jeffersonian system centering consequential legislative action on the floor. Using original data from the House Journal , we find evidence of institutional layering, with elements of gatekeeping – jurisdictional clarity, positive agenda setting, and negative agenda setting – developing unevenly and largely through changes in the behavior of members rather than formal reform of the House to empower its committees.

Rain, temperature, and votes: Weather effects on electoral participation in Argentina
articles.abstract: Compulsory voting was designed to make electoral participation immune to individual costs, yet this paper shows that rain on election day still keeps Argentine voters home. Exploiting quasi-random variation in precipitation across 526 departments and 14 national election days between 2011 and 2023, I estimate two-way fixed effects models with department and election fixed effects using ERA5 reanalysis data matched to department centroids. Each additional millimeter of voting-hours precipitation (8am–6pm) reduces turnout by 0.08 percentage points ( p < 0.01); on a day of average rainfall this implies about a 0.2 percentage-point reduction. The estimate survives an extensive identification battery: balance tests, a 9-day placebo window with horse races, grid-cell clustering, and a validation of the reanalysis data against independent rain-gauge stations. Using newly constructed vote shares by ideological bloc, I find that rainfall does not bias the partisan outcome—it leaves the incumbent vote share, the left/Peronist bloc, and the left–right balance unchanged, in contrast to the partisan effects documented under voluntary voting in Europe—and it has no effect on blank ballots, null votes, or fragmentation. Weather thus operates through the extensive margin (whether to vote) rather than the intensive margin (how to vote). If even a century-old compulsory voting institution cannot fully insulate turnout from weather shocks, institutional reforms such as postal voting, extended hours, or remote electronic voting deserve consideration even where voting is mandatory.

articles.title: Varieties of left-wing authoritarianism? The local foundations and intra-party heterogeneity of the German challenger party BSW
articles.authors: Eric Linhart, Jan Philipp Thomeczek, Manès Weisskircher, Benjamin Höhne
articles.abstract: Research has emphasized both the existence of left-wing authoritarian attitudes among the European electorate and a lack of political supply. In Germany, this dynamic changed with the rise of the BSW. Advancing research on left-wing authoritarianism in general and the BSW specifically, we rely on original Voting Advice Application (VAA) data from six city elections in 2024, allowing us to study the supply- and demand-side at the local level. We highlight three findings: First, BSW’s local-level positions vary widely across policies, including left-wing, moderate, and (moderately) right-wing stances. Second, BSW’s intra-party heterogeneity is higher on socio-cultural than on socio-economic issues. Third, BSW voters’ answers to VAA questions are more right-leaning than their self-placement. Our findings on the BSW offer key insights into an empirically observable case of left-wing authoritarianism, highlighting nuanced perspectives on the ideology of an emerging political phenomenon.

articles.title: Charisma goes viral: Péter Magyar and the digital construction of political authority
articles.authors: Rudolf Metz, Eszter Farkas, Veronika Kövesdi
articles.abstract: How is charismatic authority constructed and rewarded in digital political communication? This article develops a multidimensional framework for analysing digital charismatic signalling and applies it to Péter Magyar’s rapid political rise in Hungary. Drawing on leadership studies, social psychology and political communication, we conceptualise charisma as a relational, signalling-based process enacted through exceptional personal qualities, community construction, visionary appeals and collective challenges. Using quantitative content analysis of 486 Facebook posts published between February and June 2024, we examine how specific signals predict likes, love reactions, shares and comments. The findings show that digital charisma does not operate as a uniform engagement engine. Relational, emotional and identity-based cues generate the strongest affective engagement, especially similarity to followers, cultural-historical references, emotional mobilisation and normative-symbolic signals. Competence-oriented cues and visionary appeals have limited independent effects, while blame attribution stimulates comments. The article advances a fine-grained account of digitally mediated charismatic followership.

articles.authors: Carlos Entrena-Serrano, Trisha Meyer, Emilia Gómez, Jo Pierson
articles.abstract: This article revisits Williams’s concept of flow, Firth’s notion of algorithmic flow, and Picone et al.’s concept of Small Acts of Engagement (SAOE) to examine how users experience TikTok’s algorithmic flow. SAOE are understood as low-effort, everyday acts through which users negotiate their identities and shape their digital consumption. While SAOE have been a valuable lens for understanding user agency on earlier social media platforms, we argue that TikTok’s interface design and cultural framing introduce new challenges. The platform’s design, together with users’ perception of TikTok’s algorithmic flow as a televisual experience, reduces their SAOE to a minimal expression: a rhythm of watch, scroll, repeat , discouraging other forms of intentional, identity-driven engagement. Through a mixed-methods study combining interviews and analysis of participants’ donated TikTok data, we show how our participants experience TikTok as a place for effortless entertainment and continuous consumption, closely resembling the experience of traditional television flow.

The spectre of de-assetization: legal infrastructures and fragile fixes in fossil decommissioning
articles.abstract: Efforts to decommission coal power plants in the Global South are constrained by the legal infrastructures that create and protect them as assets. This article examines the Asian Development Bank’s Energy Transition Mechanism (ETM) as a case of managing these constraints via a series of increasingly complex and fragile spatio-temporal fixes: First, power purchase agreements and investment treaties require compensation of investors at business-as-usual asset valuations; second, for lack of public funding, this compensation is to be generated via a blended finance mechanism; third, its inability to stem these costs necessitates further legal-financial engineering, including a novel guarantee mechanism and ‘coal-to-clean’ credits. The ETM and its successive fixes are haunted by the power relations inscribed in asset creation and protection in the Global South. This renders ‘de-risked’ transition finance dubious as a blueprint for fossil decommissioning and highlights the troubled nature of climate-related asset stranding in transnational, hierarchical legal space.

Social Patterning and Spatial Variation in Intergenerational Geographic Proximity in the United Kingdom
articles.authors: Sen Li, Hill Kulu, Urška Demšar
articles.abstract: Existing understanding of intergenerational geographic proximity remains limited owing to the complexity inherent in defining geographic proximity and insufficient attention to fine‐scale spatial variation. This study focuses on children's proximity to parents, parents' proximity to adult children, and three‐generational co‐residence among individuals with both living parents and children, thereby capturing multiple kin relations and relational directionality. It further extends previous literature by examining finer‐grained spatial variation in these measures alongside individual‐ and household‐level differences. Using data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study, the results show that younger adults are more likely to co‐reside with their parents, children, or both, as expected. Higher educational attainment is associated with greater residential distance from parents and children. South Asians tend to maintain closer intergenerational ties through co‐residence or nearby residence. Spatial variation is pronounced: individuals in Northern Ireland are more likely to reside with or live near parents or adult children, whereas those in the South, such as London and the South East, are less likely to have their parents or adult children living nearby. Our findings reinforce the life course principle of linked lives, underscoring how living arrangements are interconnected across generations, and demonstrate the importance of adopting dual perspectives when examining geographic proximity within kinship dyads.

articles.title: Partnership and Fertility Trajectories of Immigrant Women Across the Migration Process to Spain: A Comparison by Country of Origin
articles.authors: Mengyao Wu, Alberto del Rey Poveda, Rafael Grande
articles.abstract: Although many studies examine family patterns among immigrants and how these differ from those in the native population, a migration‐focused perspective investigating how partnerships and childbearing trajectories intersect throughout the migration process remains scarce. Applying multichannel sequence analysis to retrospective data from the 2018 Spanish Fertility Survey, this study simultaneously analysed changes in women's partnerships and fertility behaviour around the time of migration and explored how these patterns differed by migrant origin. The pattern of family‐related migration revealed a substantial increase in cohabitation and first births shortly after migration. Cluster analysis identified five typical family trajectories among immigrant women. Multinomial logistic regression models were then used to examine how these trajectories were associated with immigrant origins. Contrary to expectations, the results did not show significant differences in these family trajectories by country of origin, except for the Early Marriage and Fertility Transitions and Single Motherhood pathways . These findings provide comprehensive insights into the interdependencies among family life domains during the migration process.

articles.title: Faith, Fear, and Belonging: Return Perceptions Among Displaced Syrian Alawites and Christians
articles.authors: Metin Gani Tapan, Necati Buğra Kuddaş, Aykut Can Demirel
articles.abstract: This study examines how displaced Syrian Alawite and Christian refugees understand return following the fall of the Assad government. Using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, it draws on in‐depth interviews with 21 refugees in Türkiye, 13 Alawites, and eight Christians. Four interconnected themes were identified: deep fears surrounding political transition and identity‐based insecurity; uncertain futures shaped by political volatility, economic survival, and fragile peace; eroded institutional belonging through exclusion from governance and public employment; and infrastructure deficits that undermine the possibility of rebuilding one's life. Alawite participants more often emphasized collective blame, retaliation, and persistent profiling because of their presumed association with the former government's actions. Christian participants placed greater emphasis on inadequate protection, distrust, and uncertainty regarding whether their political neutrality would be recognized. Concerns regarding political volatility, economic survival, renewed conflict, and public services largely converged between the two groups. The study shows that return conditions are interpreted through collective memory, religious positioning, institutional recognition, and spatial belonging rather than operating as uniform push or pull factors. Therefore, return ideation depends on whether Syria can be imagined as a safe, recognized, and sustainable place to rebuild everyday life.

articles.title: The conditional effect of autocratization: How regime change shapes international preferences in the Universal Periodic Review
articles.abstract: International organizations (IOs) are increasingly affected by autocratization of their membership. However, we still know relatively little how both episodes of democratic backsliding and autocratic consolidation affect international preferences of IO member states towards liberal norms and institutions. We argue that autocratization creates uncertainties that are consequential for how member states position themselves within IOs, but that the direction of this effect differs across regime types because of varying constraints in democracies and autocracies. Democratic backsliders are primarily concerned with domestic constraints and the risk of empowering opposition through international behavior, whereas autocratic consolidators are more focused on international audiences and reputation costs associated with autocratization. We test our argument in the specific field of human rights by employing information on the acceptance behavior of states in the Universal Period Review between 2008 and 2020. In our quantitative analysis, we find support for the proposed conditional effect of autocratization and regime type when controlling for other predictors of acceptance behavior. Autocratizing democracies are less likely to accept critical comments, whereas autocratizing autocracies are more likely. We also find that this dynamic shifts in recent years likely due to changing international attention put on democratic backsliding states. By integrating human rights and international relations scholarship, this study offers a differentiated account of when states will resist or embrace liberal norms under conditions of autocratization.

articles.title: Gatekeepers of the market? IMF surveillance and sovereign access to global finance
Randall W. Stone. 2026. Multinational Order: US Firms and International Organization (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press)
Gender, descriptive representation, and the public legitimacy of international organizations
articles.abstract: How does descriptive representation influence citizens’ perceptions of international organizations’ (IOs) legitimacy? While past work has investigated the impact of procedural and substantive dimensions on the legitimacy of IOs, the effect of descriptive representation remains largely unaddressed. We contribute to this literature by investigating whether greater gender representation increases the legitimacy of an IO when the IO governs a stereotypically “feminine” (vs. “masculine”) issue area and whether this relationship is contingent on attitudes toward gender equality. We test our expectations using pre-registered 2 × 2 factorial and conjoint experiments in Canada ( n = 1998). We find consistent evidence that individuals evaluate the legitimacy of both the IO and leader more favorably when the leader is female rather than male. Issue area and gender egalitarian attitudes attenuate the magnitude of this effect, but do not reverse it. Our article advances the study of gender representation in global governance and popular sources of IO legitimacy.

articles.title: Making Water Investible : Development Banking, Regulatory Governance, and the Institutional Production of Sanitation Infrastructure in Brazil
articles.authors: Charles Corrêa Schramm, João Paulo Nicolini Gabriel
articles.abstract: Why did long‐horizon private investment in Brazilian water and sanitation expand after 2016 despite fragmented authority and persistent political contestation? This article places the Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES) inside, rather than outside, the credible‐commitment framework. It argues that the bank operated as a credibility intermediary: it assembled service territories at investible scale, financed and coordinated project preparation, translated statutory goals into comparable contracts, and linked concessions to long‐term finance. These functions complemented courts, legislatures, the national standard‐setting role of the National Water and Basic Sanitation Agency (ANA), and post‐award supervision by infranational regulators. Process tracing of laws, concession documents, regulatory instruments, auction records, corporate filings, and attributable investor statements shows how this architecture was repeated across the Temer, Bolsonaro, and Lula administrations, albeit under different political framings. The mechanism is sequence‐sensitive but not universally necessary: Chile demonstrates an alternative route through regional utilities and a central regulator, while Colombia illustrates the continuing constraints of fragmented provision. The article also distinguishes investibility from legitimacy. Financial and contractual discipline can make commitments more legible to investors, but it neither replaces public‐law oversight nor resolves disputes over affordability, participation, and the human right to water.

articles.title: Functional Substitution and Particularized Trust: Governance Mechanisms in Hourglass Socio‐Economic Systems
articles.abstract: Governance research shows that cooperation can persist despite dysfunctional state institutions, often through trust‐based mechanisms. This paper extends these debates by examining a complex collective action problem: the engagement of small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs) in vocational education and training (VET) in post‐communist contexts. Drawing on the concept of “hourglass societies”, where trust concentrates among elites and local actors but is weak at the meso‐level, the paper argues that VET schools act as functional substitutes to meso‐level business associations by leveraging particularized trust and local networks. Evidence from Albania and Slovakia, based on 62 interviews and network analysis, demonstrates how face‐to‐face interaction, reciprocity, and localized knowledge enable SMEs to overcome prisoner's dilemma dynamics. These findings contribute to governance theory by showing how functional substitution and micro‐level trust structures sustain cooperation in fragmented socio‐economic systems, offering insights for designing policies for collective good provision such as education politics beyond Western contexts.

articles.title: Compound and heterogeneous relationships between climate extremes and global net migration
articles.authors: Kristina Petrova, Karim Zantout, Sandra Zimmermann, Venla Niva, Matti Kummu, Katja Frieler, Jacob Schewe
articles.abstract: Climate extremes are increasingly disrupting livelihoods and shaping patterns of human mobility. Their longer-term and compounding relationships with migration remain understudied, particularly at the subnational scale. In this study, by analysing global subnational net migration data, we show that associations between climate extremes and migration vary by hazard type, timing, consecutive events, income level and pre-existing migration context. Floods are associated with decreased net migration across contexts, with effects lasting several years and appearing stronger in lower-income areas. Droughts, by contrast, show associations with net migration primarily in higher-income settings, with effects generally short-term. Tropical cyclones correspond to decreased net migration primarily in lower-income areas, with effects lasting over several years. For compound exposure, droughts show the clearest patterns, with prolonged exposure linked to reduced migration inflows in population-attracting areas. These results highlight how climate extremes interact with local socioeconomic contexts to shape mobility.

articles.title: Modeling Civic Engagement in the Age of AI: A Communication Mediation Approach to AI News, Multifaceted Trust, and Participation in a Two-Wave Panel Study
articles.authors: Seungahn Nah, Fanjue Liu, Jun Luo, Lee LaPlaca, Chris DeFelice
articles.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes both a topic of news coverage and a force shaping the information environment, citizens must make sense of AI-related issues while evaluating machine-generated content, journalistic coverage, and institutional actors. This study applies the Orientation-Stimulus-Reasoning-Orientation-Response framework to examine how AI-related news consumption is associated with interpersonal discussion, multifaceted trust, and AI-related offline civic participation. Using two-wave panel data from U.S. adults (Wave 1 = 2,010; Wave 2 = 942), the study models AI-related news consumption across television, newspapers, online news sites, and social media as the stimulus; AI-related online and offline discussion as reasoning; trust in AI-generated news, legacy media coverage of AI, and AI-related institutional actors as reorientation; and AI-related offline civic participation as the response. Results reveal a selective communication pathway. Newspaper and social media AI news use were the most consistent predictors of AI-related discussion. Online discussion was associated with later trust in AI-generated news and legacy media coverage of AI, and trust in AI-generated news and AI-related institutional actors was associated with later offline participation. The observed indirect pathways operated through online discussion and trust in AI-generated news. These findings refine communication mediation research by showing that public engagement with AI-related issues depends on where people encounter AI news, how they discuss it, and which sources and institutions they come to trust.

articles.title: Chronic loneliness and isolation phenotypes and physical and mental health in older adults
articles.authors: Yuteng Ma, Jessica K. Bone, Rosie Mayston, Qian Gao
articles.abstract: Chronic social deficits (persistent feelings of being lonely or isolated) have been linked to premature mortality, yet the underlying physical and mental pathways remain unclear. This study used data from 4,090 older adults in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, a longitudinal panel study. Using outcome-wide analyses, we assessed how the chronicity of social deficits was associated with 17 health outcomes across physical, mental, cognitive and behavioural health domains. Regression models showed that chronic loneliness was longitudinally associated with increased risks of worse general health, functional capacity, and mental wellbeing, and more unhealthy behaviours. Chronic isolation and onset of isolation were associated with lower quality of life, whereas isolation remission was positively related to enhanced mental wellbeing and cognition compared to no isolation. Findings suggest an association between chronicity of loneliness and adverse health outcomes, highlighting chronic social deficits as an important correlate of healthy ageing.

articles.title: Cognitive appeal promotes the persistence of inefficient solutions and hinders cumulative cultural evolution
articles.authors: Ali Seyhun Saral, Manvir Singh, Antoine Jacquet, Haneul Jang, Maxime Derex
articles.abstract: Through cumulative cultural evolution, human populations discover novel solutions that allow them to solve complex problems. However, populations also reliably develop and sustain practices that are costly yet appear to have no effect on their stated outcome, such as bloodletting, divination, and malicious sorcery. Here, we show that ineffective, costly solutions can develop and be maintained because of their cognitive appeal. In a pre-registered transmission-chain experiment, participants were tasked with developing a solution to a problem over several trials, after which they passed instructions onto the subsequent generation. The visual appearance of the experimental task was manipulated to vary the extent to which cognitive biases could interfere with participants’ expectations of efficacy, enabling a direct test of the effect of cognitive appeal on cumulative cultural evolution. Participants in the low-appeal treatment ( n = 240) progressively develop more efficient solutions across generations. Participants in the high-appeal treatment ( n = 240), in contrast, produce costlier solutions, and we did not observe a statistically significant increase in efficiency over the course of the experiment. These results suggest that, even under conditions favorable to cumulative cultural evolution, a form of cognitive appeal can alone prevent the process and promote the emergence and cultural persistence of ineffective solutions.

articles.title: Wildfire exposure and political participation in Africa
articles.authors: Siyuan Chen, Michael Akwasi Appiah-Kubi, Lina Meng, Pengfei Liu, Lu Lin
articles.abstract: Civic engagement can shape collective responses to climate change. However, evidence on how climate-related disasters affect political participation in Africa remains limited. Combining Global Fire Atlas records with Afrobarometer surveys of more than 100,000 people in 34 African countries, we show that people living close to wildfires are more likely to vote, contact local councillors, attend community meetings, and raise collective issues, whereas protest participation shows weaker responses. These effects are larger in arid regions and among people with higher climate literacy or access to information, members of politically dominant ethnic groups and those living near ethnic boundaries. Our findings suggest that participation is motivated mainly by immediate material loss and demand for public services, rather than environmental concern. These findings highlight the importance of addressing post-disaster needs to sustain political engagement and public support for long-term climate adaptation in the Global South.

articles.title: The Corpus of English–Tagalog Code-switching: an integrative corpus of linguistic contact effects
articles.abstract: The Corpus of English–Tagalog Code-switching (CEnTaCS) is a new corpus designed to document naturalistic English–Tagalog bilingual speech. Locally referred to as Taglish, it is a widely-used yet understudied contact variety in the Philippines. Recorded in 2025 in Metro Manila, the corpus comprises three interrelated datasets: individual story retelling recordings, cognitive control data based on the Arrow Flanker task, and sociolinguistic questionnaire data. CEnTaCS offers fine-grained data on code-switching across clausal, lexical, and morphemic levels, with particular attention to intra-word code-switching, a salient but still insufficiently documented feature of Taglish. Beyond code-switching, the corpus captures a broad range of language contact phenomena, including borrowing, calquing, convergence, and interference. By making these data systematically available, the corpus supports an integrated account of mixed-language practices that brings together structural, cognitive, and sociolinguistic perspectives. CEnTaCS thus enables researchers to investigate how contact-induced structures are constrained linguistically, how they relate to bilingual processing, and how they index social meaning and identity in a community where bilingualism is deeply embedded in everyday life.

articles.title: It Doesn’t Take Extremes to Trigger Hate: A Mixed-Methods Study on Meme Extremity and User Comments on 9GAG
articles.abstract: Users engage with socially and politically relevant topics by sharing memes and adopting the creative styles of meme-sharing platforms like 9GAG. Although memes can contain political critique, research also linked them to hate speech and increasingly extreme content. Little attention has been paid to entertainment-first platforms, where (perceived) homogeneity, anonymity, and humor-driven social norms may shape how political and hateful content is produced and discussed in the comment section. This study addresses this gap using a sequential mixed-methods design. First, we analyzed 343 memes on 9GAG with quantitative content analysis, categorizing them into classes based on varying degrees of extreme content using latent class analysis. Second, via qualitative content analysis, we investigated the comment sections of six memes representing each identified class to determine how extreme content levels influence hateful comments. Results show that anonymity and ingroup identity foster a climate in which hate is normalized and often obscured through humor. However, even purely humorous memes provoked hateful comments, suggesting that factors beyond meme extremity, like topic sensitivity and referenced outgroups, also shape hateful follow-up communication.

articles.title: How Definitions Shape Our Understanding of Political Influencers on Social Media
articles.authors: Jennifer Oser, John Wagner, Nir Grinberg
articles.abstract: Political discourse now circulates through sprawling social media networks where multiple actors wield influence in addition to traditional elites. Yet scholarly conclusions about who actually shapes that discourse diverge because leading studies operationalize “political influencer” in fundamentally different ways. To clarify the stakes of those choices—and advance more coherent theorizing—we examine six definitions that are prevalent in the literature and are rooted in audience size, elite ties, network importance, and message engagement. We then apply these distinctive definitions to a single dataset, namely a panel of 597,815 registered U.S. voters on Twitter during the 2020 presidential campaign to identify convergence and divergence across definitions. Three patterns emerge. First, conceptual boundaries matter: definitions that differ in scale rarely converge on the same influencers, confirming that different lenses reveal largely distinct influencer groups. Second, definitional emphasis reshapes the portrait of influence itself: elite-based criteria surface highly political, centrally positioned senders with compact but engaged followings, whereas follower- and engagement-based criteria net vastly larger, more heterogeneous groups that address politics only episodically. Third, upstream choices about conceptual boundaries and definitional emphases cascade downstream to the characteristics of influencers’ audiences, producing systematic shifts in followers’ age, gender, racial, and partisan characteristics. By showing how conceptual decisions impact both who counts as a political influencer and which citizens follow their messages, this study lays the groundwork for clearer conceptualization of the relevant dimensions for advancing the accumulation of knowledge on this increasingly important political phenomenon.

articles.title: Visibility, Sovereignty, and the Affective Politics of Media: Decolonial Struggles Over Representation and Reception During the 2022 Indigenous Protests in Ecuador
articles.abstract: This article examines how visibility, affect, and epistemic power intersected during the June 2022 Indigenous-led protests in Ecuador, when media became a central terrain of struggle over meaning and legitimacy. Combining multimodal media analysis with ethnographically informed audience research, the study compares three communicative regimes: government, commercial, and Indigenous/community media, to show how each enacted distinct infrastructures of visibility and political intelligibility. Government media constructed visibility as surveillance, framing dissent as a crisis of order through securitized language, ritualized imagery, and affective scripts that moved audiences from fear to reassurance. Commercial broadcasters pursued legitimacy through moderation, translating protest into economic disruption and containing conflict through the aesthetics of balance and procedural neutrality. In contrast, Indigenous/community media operating through platformed livestreams enacted visibility as relational sovereignty, embedding communication within collective action, historical continuity, and participatory verification. Drawing on decolonial media theory and scholarship on affective publics and Indigenous digital activism, the article conceptualizes media as ontopolitical infrastructures that organize not only information but the conditions under which political subjects and truths become recognizable. Reception data from Kichwa-speaking communities demonstrate that Indigenous audiences engaged in collective practices of interpretation, verification, and refusal. Affective responses such as anger and pride functioned as epistemic resources, transforming exposure into critique and reception into communal knowledge-making. The article advances a decolonial reframing of visibility as infrastructure and theorizes reception as epistemic labor sustaining narrative sovereignty.

articles.title: A DuBoisian Approach to Civic Education
articles.abstract: This article presents a DuBosian approach to civic education: one that advocates for content that is racially inclusive and addresses political activism; centers conversations about politics; and ensures that K-12 educators reflect the diversity of their students. I argue that this approach provides a useful framework for classroom practices that can equip young people with the capacity needed to navigate and transform a democratic system defined by persistent racial inequality. I also assess whether there is public support for such an approach using a national sample of Americans. I find that a majority of respondents across racial, ethnic, and partisan lines, including many parents, support central tenets of a DuBoisian approach to civic education. By emphasizing the tangible pedagogical techniques associated with a DuBosian approach to civic education, it may be possible to sidestep the ambiguity and polarization of curriculum debates and reengage in the nuances of civic education policymaking.

articles.title: Does cross-border engagement shape emotional identification? Exploring the link between dimensions of transnational engagement and the feeling of belonging among intra-European migrants
articles.abstract: Public debates increasingly link immigrants’ national belonging to their cross-border engagement. Using survey data on six intra-European origin groups in Switzerland (first and second generation), we examine how four dimensions of transnational practices and relations —return intentions, social, political, and economic ties—relate to identification with the country of residence (CoR) and the country of origin (CoO). Unlike previous research, that has often led to inconclusive findings, we study different dimensions of transnational engagement and their heterogenous logics separately in their relation to both the identification with the CoO and the CoR based on representative data. Our findings demonstrate that the diverse dimensions of transnational activities and relations differ in their association with identification. This underscores the need to analytically separate these dimensions. In addition, several of these dimensions covary with identification with the CoO, but only one clearly covaries with identification with the CoR. This indicates that transnational engagement with the CoO and integration into the CoR are to a considerable extent, different worlds for intra-European migrants.

articles.abstract: Experts widely agree that East Asian cultures are more collectivistic than Western cultures. Yet 76 survey studies found no reliable difference. Our explanation is that the most-used surveys are contaminated with ‘warm fuzzy’ items, which describe warmth and prosociality towards everyone near and far. We argue that collectivism is better understood as ‘responsibilism’, which emphasizes responsibilities in close relationships. A survey found that many cultural psychologists expect collectivistic cultures to agree with warm fuzzy items. Then we developed a responsibilism scale and tested 12,247 people in 100 cultures. Results showed large cultural differences ( d = 3.98 [2.50, 5.43]) that were previously obscured by flawed measurement. Responsibilism predicted differences across societies (such as family ties and corruption) and individuals (social class and politics) that most earlier scales missed. This study offers a solution to previous puzzling findings by distinguishing warm fuzzy prosociality from responsibilism and introducing a scale with stronger predictive validity.
